A method whose result is another kind of object, such as Ray.intersectPlane or Box.getCenter, takes an out too. Without one, it creates a new object on each call. A node is any object in the 3D scene. Methods of nodes and views that return a point or a ray, such as getGlobalPosition and screenToRay, work the same way. A method that reads a point takes a PointData3D, which is any object with x, y and z, such as a node's position or a plain { x: 0, y: 1, z: 0 }.

Each object you create in a frame and then drop, whether with new Vector3() or from a method, is garbage. The browser collects it later, and that can make the frame rate stutter. In a ticker callback or a pointer listener, create what you need once, outside it, and pass it as out. Here an enemy chases the player at two units a second. Both have the same parent, so their positions are in the same space: const toPlayer = new Vector3(); app.ticker.add((ticker) => { player.position.subtract(enemy.position, toPlayer).normalize(); // the direction, length 1 enemy.position.addScaledVector(toPlayer, 2 * (ticker.deltaMS / 1000)); }); A node's position, rotation and scale are ObservableVector3s, and its quaternion is an ObservableQuaternion. They have the same methods as Vector3 and Quaternion. To keep a copy, use new Vector3().copyFrom(node.position) rather than clone. A clone is still tied to the node, so each write to it marks the node changed.

A Quaternion holds a rotation as four numbers that you don't work out yourself. setFromAxisAngle builds a turn by an angle around an axis, given as a direction of length 1. Multiplying two quaternions combines their turns. Scene graph and transforms covers when a node uses its quaternion and when its rotation. On a node, multiply adds a turn around the node's own axes, which turn with the node, and premultiply adds it around the parent's axes. In a loaded model, each node's quaternion holds the rotation from the file, so multiply that quaternion to turn the node further. To lean a car's body, copy its quaternion once after loading and start each frame again from that copy, so the lean doesn't build up from frame to frame: const body = car.getChildByLabel('body', true)!; const rest = new Quaternion().copyFrom(body.quaternion); // the turn the file gave the body const roll = new Quaternion(); const forward = { x: 0, y: 0, z: 1 }; app.ticker.add(() => { roll.setFromAxisAngle(forward, lean); // lean: an angle in radians that your code works out body.quaternion.copyFrom(rest).multiply(roll); // around the body's own z axis }); For a turn that keeps going, such as a spinning wheel, build each frame's turn from the time the frame took and multiply it in: spin.setFromAxisAngle(axle, speed * (ticker.deltaMS / 1000)), then wheel.quaternion.multiply(spin). slerp moves part of the way from one rotation toward another, the shorter way round. If you ease a car's angle toward a new heading instead, you have to keep the gap between -180° and 180°, or the car spins the long way round. A slerp needs no such check: const up = { x: 0, y: 1, z: 0 }; const heading = new Quaternion(); app.ticker.add((ticker) => { heading.setFromAxisAngle(up, targetYaw); // close the same share of the gap each second, whatever the frame rate car.quaternion.slerp(heading, 1 - Math.exp(-3 * (ticker.deltaMS / 1000))); }); If you turn a node with multiply, slerp or another quaternion method, set its other turns through the quaternion too, rather than through rotation. For example, set its starting turn with setFromAxisAngle.

Most code needs no matrix of its own. Each node keeps its worldTransform, the matrix that places it in the world. The view updates that matrix when it draws, so it can be out of date, such as right after you add or move the node. getGlobalTransform computes an up-to-date one. Scene graph says when to use each. toGlobal and toLocal move points between spaces. You build your own Matrix4 to place each mesh in a BatchedMesh3D, which draws many meshes from one node. Batched meshes does this with compose. You also build one to move a shape between spaces, as Shapes shows. Two things to know: In a.multiply(b), b applies to a point first. getInverse(m) sets the matrix you call it on to the inverse of m, the matrix that undoes m.

A Ray starts at its origin and runs along its direction. The sphere tests and distances assume the direction has length 1, so call normalize() on it after you set it yourself. screenToRay builds a ray through a point on the screen. To find the node under that point, use pointer events or raycast. Interaction covers both. A Plane is a flat surface that goes on for ever. View3D uses one to find the ground under the pointer. A Box is lined up with the axes, from its min corner to its max corner. getLocalBounds returns a node's bounds as a box. A Sphere is a centre and a radius. A mesh's boundingSphere is one. Meshes shows how to test it against the camera's frustum, the volume the camera sees. A shape keeps the vectors you pass to its constructor, so new Sphere(enemy.position, 2) shares the enemy's position, and moving the sphere moves the enemy. Pass new vectors instead, such as new Vector3().copyFrom(enemy.position). Each shape is in some space. A ray from screenToRay and a mesh's boundingSphere are in world space, while getLocalBounds and a geometry's bounds3D are in the node's own space. Move one into the other's space before you test them: applyMatrix4 with the node's world matrix takes a shape from the node's space to world space. A box grows when the matrix turns it, since Box.applyMatrix4 fits a new box, lined up with the world axes, around the turned one. Pass a box to write into, as in mesh.geometry.bounds3D.applyMatrix4(mesh.worldTransform, worldBounds). Without one, applyMatrix4 changes the geometry's own bounds, which pointer events, raycast and every mesh that shares the geometry read. For an exact test, move the ray into the node's space instead, with ray.applyMatrix4(inverse.getInverse(mesh.worldTransform), localRay). Here inverse is a Matrix4 and localRay is a Ray, and you create both once. Writing into localRay keeps ray in world space for the next node. Ray.applyMatrix4 keeps the direction at length 1, so on a scaled node a distance along the moved ray isn't a world distance. To compare hits on several nodes, take each hit point back to world space with applyMatrix4(mesh.worldTransform).

seededRandom returns a function to call in place of Math.random. The same seed gives the same numbers in the same order, so a scene laid out with it comes out the same on every load. The seed is a string. Here each level scatters its trees the same way every time: const random = seededRandom(`level-${level}`); for (const tree of trees) { tree.position.set((random() - 0.5) * 200, 0, (random() - 0.5) * 200); tree.rotation.y = random() * Math.PI * 2; } A particle system takes a seeded random function through its createRandom option. Pass a function that creates one, such as () => seededRandom('stream') in Bursts on demand. Particles covers what a seed makes repeat.
Scene graph and transforms: positions, rotations and the spaces nodes are in. View3D and 2D content: from the screen to rays and points in the world, and back. Interaction: hit volumes and picking.

PixiJS 3D loads glTF 2.0, an open file format for 3D models. A model comes either as a .gltf file, which is JSON that can point to buffer and image files beside it, or as one binary .glb file. Importing @pixi/3d registers loaders for both with PixiJS's Assets, so a model loads like any other asset: import { Model3D } from '@pixi/3d'; import type { Scene3DSource } from '@pixi/3d'; import { Assets } from 'pixi.js'; const source = await Assets.load<Scene3DSource>('car.glb'); const car = new Model3D(source); view3d.root.addChild(car); Drop a .glb file of your own on Model viewer to see it load.

Assets.load returns a Scene3DSource, which holds the file's geometry, materials, textures and animation clips. A Model3D uses the source to build the file's scene as nodes under itself. Nodes are the 3D counterpart of 2D containers. The model, not the source, is what you add to your scene. Each model builds its own nodes and shares the source's geometry, materials and textures, the way 2D sprites share a texture. A second model loads nothing, so several copies of a prop cost one load: const crate = await Assets.load<Scene3DSource>('crate.glb'); for (const x of [-2, 0, 2]) { const model = new Model3D(crate); model.position.x = x; view3d.root.addChild(model); } For thousands of copies, Choosing a node for many objects compares the other ways to draw them. Because models share materials, changing one changes every model that draws it. Every model built from the source draws the source's materials until you give it materials of its own. source.material holds the file's named materials, keyed by name: source.material['Paint'].baseColor = 0x3366ff; // tints the paint on every car that draws the source's Paint To change one model alone, give it materials of its own with materials. clone copies a material with everything the file gave it, textures included, then sets the options you pass: const redCar = new Model3D({ source, materials: { Paint: source.material['Paint'].clone({ baseColor: 0xd81b3c }) }, }); A record replaces materials by name, as here. An array replaces them by index into source.materials, and a function runs once for each of them. Assigning model.materials switches the materials of a model that's already built, and assigning undefined gives it the source's materials back. Neither the option nor the assignment destroys the materials it replaces, so destroy your copies when you're done with them. Materials per model dissolves one of three helmets this way. Model3DOptions set up a model as it's built. Pass them in place of the source, with the source as source. castShadow and receiveShadow apply to every mesh in it, and autoPlay starts a clip: const water = new Model3D({ source: waterSource, castShadow: false, receiveShadow: false }); const fox = new Model3D({ source: foxSource, autoPlay: 'Walk' }); A model keeps the size its file was built at. glTF works in metres, but some files ignore that. The fox in Quick start is about 80 units tall. Measuring and sizing shows how to scale a model to the size you want.

Meshes and materials. A glTF mesh is made of one or more parts, each with its own material. A mesh with one part becomes a Mesh3D, and a mesh with several becomes a Container3D holding one Mesh3D per part. Materials load as Material3D. A material the file marks unlit loads as a FlatMaterial, which ignores lights. Names. Each node takes its name in the file as its label, or node_<index> when it has none. A mesh's own name in the file labels nothing. The parts of a mesh with several parts get no name from the file either. To find them, look up the container that holds them by the name of the node the mesh sits on. Parents and children shows how getChildByLabel finds a node by label, and why it can miss the bones a character's mesh bends with. To see what a file holds, logHierarchy prints the tree to the console: car.logHierarchy(); // For Khronos's ToyCar sample, it prints: // Model3D "Model3D" // Mesh3D "ToyCar" // Mesh3D "Fabric" // Mesh3D "Glass" // Camera3D "Camera001" // ... Cameras. The file's cameras become Camera3D nodes where the file placed them, listed in model.cameras. Switching cameras shows how to draw from one. Lights. The file's lights become DirectionalLight, PointLight and SpotLight nodes. Like lights you make, they cast no shadows until you turn on a directional or spot light's castShadow. Point lights cast none. Animation. When the file has animation clips, the model's player plays them. The player is undefined when the file has none. Animation covers playing them.

View3D.from builds a view around a source. The view's root is a Model3D built from the source, so view3d.root is the model: import { View3D } from '@pixi/3d'; const view3d = View3D.from(source, { autoResize: true, environment: sky }); app.stage.addChild(view3d); view3d.root.player?.play('Walk'); The view comes ready to draw the model: Its camera is the camera you pass, or else the file's first camera. A file with none gets a new camera on the model's +Z side, facing it, just far enough back to fit the whole model in view. When the file brings no lights, the view adds a DirectionalLight as a child of the camera, so it lights whatever the camera faces. Pass light: false to light the scene yourself. View3DFromOptions takes the view's options and the model's, such as castShadow and autoPlay, in one object. To let people turn the model, aim an OrbitCamera at its centre, as Orbit camera shows.
documents.s: Showing one model on its own

documents.t: glTF extensions add features to the format. PixiJS 3D reads these: Extension What it brings KHR_materials_clearcoat, KHR_materials_sheen, KHR_materials_specular, KHR_materials_iridescence, KHR_materials_anisotropy, KHR_materials_ior Material features; see Physical extensions KHR_materials_transmission, KHR_materials_volume Glass; see Transmission and volume KHR_materials_emissive_strength A stronger glow; see Glow KHR_materials_unlit Materials that ignore lights, as FlatMaterial KHR_texture_transform Tiled and offset textures, one transform per material KHR_texture_basisu, EXT_texture_avif, EXT_texture_webp KTX2, AVIF and WebP textures KHR_lights_punctual Directional, point and spot lights KHR_node_visibility Nodes the file hides start hidden KHR_draco_mesh_compression, EXT_meshopt_compression, KHR_meshopt_compression, KHR_mesh_quantization Compressed geometry; see Compressed models KTX2 textures, which the GPU can keep compressed, need PixiJS's KTX2 loader. Import it once, before you load the model: import 'pixi.js/ktx2'; Without it, the loader uses a texture's other image if it has one. A texture with only a KTX2 image fails the load, and the error names the import. PixiJS 3D supports no other extension. You may meet these three: EXT_mesh_gpu_instancing repeats a mesh. Only the original draws, at its node. KHR_materials_pbrSpecularGlossiness is an older material model. The loader ignores it, so you lose any colours and textures kept in it. KHR_animation_pointer lets clips animate materials, lights and cameras. A file that uses it doesn't load yet, so leave it out when you export.

Destroying a model stops its clips and takes it out of the scene, but leaves the source, which other models may share. Don't pass it flags that destroy geometry, materials or textures. Destroying explains why. To free a file, destroy every model built from it, then unload the file through Assets, as you would a 2D texture. Unloading destroys the source's geometry, materials and textures: car.destroy({ children: true }); await Assets.unload('car.glb'); For a view from View3D.from, destroy the view with children: true, which destroys its model too. A material you gave a model is yours. Unloading the file leaves it, so destroy it once no model uses it. A file can keep its images beside it rather than inside it. Those images load through Assets by URL, so unloading the file destroys them for anything else that loaded the same image, such as the other models in a kit that share one texture atlas. Unload a kit's files together, once none of its models is drawn. To free GPU memory for a while but keep the model, take it out of the scene and call unload. Adding it back uploads it again. The call unloads the source's geometry and materials, which every model built from that source shares, so take all of those models out of the scene before the next frame. Unloading says how much of that memory comes back. view3d.root.removeChild(car); car.unload();
Compressed models: smaller downloads with meshopt and Draco. Animation: playing and blending the clips a model brings. Environment and IBL: lighting a model from a picture of its surroundings.

Three kinds of glTF extension make a model's meshes smaller. Meshopt and Draco compress the file, and the loader decodes it as it loads. Mesh quantization stores vertex data as small integers, which the GPU reads as they are. PixiJS 3D reads all three, so a compressed file loads with the same Assets.load call as any other: const source = await Assets.load<Scene3DSource>('fox-meshopt.glb'); Extension What it makes smaller Decoder EXT_meshopt_compression, KHR_meshopt_compression The download Comes with @pixi/3d KHR_draco_mesh_compression The download Fetched from Google the first time a file needs it KHR_mesh_quantization The download and GPU memory None Quantization works with either of the others. None of the three compresses textures, so a file that's mostly images shrinks little. For files you compress yourself, gltfpack applies meshopt and quantization in one command, and can compress textures too. Compression loads a different sample model compressed each of these ways.
The loader imports meshopt's decoder the first time a file needs it, so there's nothing to set up. Meshopt compresses a file's animation clips as well as its meshes.

In Compression, the walking Cesium Man and the sunglasses are Draco files. The loader fetches the Draco decoder from Google's servers. To host the decoder yourself, for example in an app that works offline, copy the two files at the URLs in dracoDecoderUrls to your server. Then pass their new URLs to setDracoDecoderPath before the first Draco file loads, since the loader reads the URLs when it first decodes a Draco mesh: import { setDracoDecoderPath } from '@pixi/3d'; setDracoDecoderPath({ jsUrl: '/draco/draco_wasm_wrapper.js', wasmUrl: '/draco/draco_decoder.wasm', }); Draco meshes load without their morph targets, the extra shapes a mesh can blend toward. For a model that has them, run gltfpack on the uncompressed original with the morph target flags, since gltfpack can't read a Draco file.

KHR_mesh_quantization stores vertex data, such as positions, normals and texture coordinates, as 8- or 16-bit integers rather than 32-bit floats. The default hit test checks a mesh's bounding box, and it works on a quantized mesh too. A per-triangle hit test finds the triangle under the pointer, but it never hits a mesh with integer positions (HitVolume3DInput). A hit's uv is a texture coordinate only on a mesh whose texture coordinates are floats. gltfpack can keep either as floats, as Compressing your own models shows. gltfpack quantizes texture coordinates by default. When it does, it adds a texture transform to each textured material, which maps the quantized coordinates back onto the texture. The loader sets that transform as the material's uvTransform, so a textured material you build yourself needs the same transform, or it samples the wrong part of the texture. To give one model a material of its own, clone the file's material, which keeps the transform: const blueFox = new Model3D({ source, materials: (material) => material.clone({ baseColor: 0x99aaff }), // tints this fox alone });

gltfpack, from the meshoptimizer project, compresses a glTF or GLB file with meshopt and quantizes it in one command: npx gltfpack -i model.glb -o model-packed.glb -cc -c compresses with meshopt, and -cc compresses further. Quantization is on by default, and -noq turns it off. gltfpack also rearranges the file so it draws faster, and that changes what your code finds in it: It merges meshes and materials, and drops the nodes it doesn't need. A node is the 3D counterpart of a 2D container. These changes can remove a name your code looks up with getChildByLabel or source.material. -kn keeps named nodes, and -km keeps named materials. gltfpack drops every mesh and texture name whatever the flags, so source.geometry and source.texture come back empty. Reach a mesh through its node and a texture through its material instead. With integer positions, it can move a mesh to an unnamed child of the node -kn keeps, so getChildByLabel returns a Container3D rather than the Mesh3D. -vpf keeps positions as floats and each mesh on its named node. Per-triangle hit tests need -vpf too. -vtf keeps texture coordinates as floats, for a hit's uv. The loader skips morph target data stored as integers, so add -vpf -vnf for a model that has morph targets. If your code looks up parts of a model by name or hit-tests it per triangle, compress it with a command like this one: npx gltfpack -i car.glb -o car-packed.glb -cc -kn -km -vpf -tc turns textures into KTX2, a format the GPU can keep compressed. The npm build of gltfpack can't write KTX2, so download a native build from its releases page. Those textures have no PNG or JPEG to fall back on, so the app needs PixiJS's KTX2 loader. That loader fetches the code that converts KTX2 for the GPU from jsDelivr, unless PixiJS's setKTXTranscoderPath points it elsewhere.
Loading models: sources, models and what a file can bring. Performance: what else keeps a scene fast on phones.

A particle is a small flat card, such as a spark or a snowflake, that turns to face the camera by default. PixiJS 3D draws particles two ways: ParticleSystem3D, from @pixi/3d/extras, emits particles and moves them on its own, as its options describe. ParticleContainer3D, from @pixi/3d, draws particles where your code puts them. A particle system is a particle container with the behaviour built in. Each draws all its particles in one draw call.

This system makes a campfire's flames: import { ConeShape, ParticleSystem3D } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; import { Texture } from 'pixi.js'; // A soft white dot, drawn on a canvas const canvas = document.createElement('canvas'); canvas.width = canvas.height = 128; const context = canvas.getContext('2d')!; const gradient = context.createRadialGradient(64, 64, 0, 64, 64, 64); gradient.addColorStop(0, 'rgba(255,255,255,1)'); gradient.addColorStop(0.22, 'rgba(255,255,255,0.55)'); gradient.addColorStop(1, 'rgba(255,255,255,0)'); context.fillStyle = gradient; context.fillRect(0, 0, 128, 128); const dot = Texture.from(canvas); const flames = new ParticleSystem3D({ texture: dot, blendMode: 'add', billboard: 'cylindrical', capacity: 120, // emitRate times the longest life, 110 × 1, rounded up emitRate: 110, shape: new ConeShape({ angle: 12, radius: 0.22 }), life: [0.5, 1], speed: [1.5, 2.3], size: [0.5, 0.85], sizeEnd: [0.05, 0.2], alpha: 0.7, alphaEnd: 0, color: 0xffd98a, colorEnd: 0xd12b06, drag: 1.6, }); flames.position.y = 0.2; view3d.root.addChild(flames); A system starts emitting as soon as you create it and updates itself every frame. Add it under view3d.root to see it. Leave out texture and each particle is a solid square of its color. Particle system changes a running system's rate, shape, gravity and drag from a panel. A system has a fixed number of slots, one per particle. That number is its capacity. The system fills the slots in turn, so once it has used them all, a new particle takes the oldest particle's slot, even if that particle is still alive. Make the capacity big enough to hold every particle born within the longest life, or particles vanish early. For a steady stream, that's about emitRate times the longest life. Don't go far past it, because the GPU works on every slot each frame, live or empty, and the view draws a system even when it's off screen.

ParticleSystem3DOptions lists every option. Numbers set per particle, such as life, size and speed, take one value or a [min, max] range. Each particle picks a value from the range when it's born. color and colorEnd take one colour each. Where they start. shape sets where each particle starts and which way it moves. It's a PointShape by default. Use a ConeShape for flames and smoke, a SphereShape for bursts, a BoxShape for snow, or your own EmitterShape. The point, cone and box send particles up, so rotate the system to aim them another way. How they move. speed is how fast particles leave along the shape's direction. It's 0 by default, so without speed or gravity, particles stay where they're born. A positive number for gravity pulls particles down, and a negative one lifts them. An { x, y, z } value sets the acceleration directly, so gravity: 9.8 is the same as { x: 0, y: -9.8, z: 0 }. drag slows particles down. How they change. sizeEnd, alphaEnd and colorEnd set the value each particle reaches at the end of its life, and spin rotates it. Leave one out and the particle keeps its starting value. Each one you set adds work to the shader, so set only what the effect needs. How they look. color multiplies the texture, as a 2D tint does, so draw the sprite white and colour it here. A blendMode of 'add' brightens what's behind, so overlapping flames add up to a brighter glow. A billboard of 'cylindrical' keeps flames upright as the camera tilts. They get thinner the further the camera looks down, and vanish when it looks straight down. A billboard of 'horizontal' lays particles flat on the ground, for rings. Pass texture an array of frames from one sprite sheet and each particle gets a random frame by default. Set frameMode to 'animate' or 'overLife' to play the frames as a flipbook. A flipbook needs the frames laid out as a grid of equal cells, left to right from the top left. With a packed atlas, a flipbook can play the wrong cells. size is a diameter in world units, not pixels, and scaling the system doesn't change it. Particles are unlit. Lights don't reach them, and they don't cast or receive shadows. Fire and smoke shows the three billboard modes, the blend modes and flipbook frames on a campfire.

stop stops emitting and lets live particles finish their lives. play starts emitting again. clear removes every live particle at once. You can change emitRate at any time, but size the capacity for the highest rate. You can change gravity and drag too, but assign a new value. Editing gravity.x in place doesn't reach the particles. The system works out each particle's path from the moment that particle was born, so changing either one moves every particle already in the air, not only new ones. spawn emits particles right away, whether the system is playing or stopped. It can override some options for that batch, and takes velocity in place of speed. ParticleSpawnOverrides lists which options. With emitRate: 0, a system emits only what you spawn and what its bursts release on a schedule. In the shooting gallery tutorial, confetti spawns where the player hits a target: target.eventMode = 'static'; target.on('pointerdown', (e) => { if (e.hit3D) confetti.spawn(12, { position: e.hit3D.point, color: 0xffc93c }); }); position puts the batch at a point in the world, not at the system, so one system handles every hit. A system updates on pixi's Ticker.shared, not your app.ticker, unless you create the app with sharedTicker: true. So pausing or slowing app.ticker doesn't pause or slow the particles. To keep a system in step with your game, create it with autoUpdate: false and call update from your own loop. Setting app.ticker.speed to 0 then freezes the particles. const smoke = new ParticleSystem3D({ ...smokeOptions, autoUpdate: false }); app.ticker.add((ticker) => smoke.update(ticker)); time is the system's clock in seconds. Set it, forwards or backwards, to show any moment the slots still hold. Setting it doesn't emit particles. To scrub through time, turn off autoUpdate. Before you turn it back on, set time to the latest moment the system reached, or the particles born after the moment you picked show twice. Give a system createRandom: () => seededRandom('fireworks') and it draws the same random values in the same order every run, so gotoAndPlay(0) replays the same burst. seededRandom makes the generator. Bursts on demand puts these calls on buttons, spawns where you tap and scrubs time.

By default a particle lives in world space. It starts wherever the system is when it's born and doesn't follow the system after that. Move a chimney and the smoke already in the air stays where it was. With space: 'local', particles move, rotate and scale with their system. Use it for effects such as a glow that follows a moving orb. Gravity then acts in the system's own space too, so in a system turned upside down it pulls particles up. Positions you write into a particle container or pass to spawn use the same space.

The particles in one system draw in slot order, not sorted by distance. With a blendMode of 'normal', a far particle drawn later covers a near one. 'add', 'screen' and 'multiply' look the same in any order. For hard-edged particles such as leaves, alphaMode: 'mask' cuts each one out along its texture's edge, so the nearer particle covers the farther one. When the view sorts a system against other blended meshes, it treats the system as one object at the system's position, wherever its particles have gone.

A ParticleContainer3D draws particles that something else moves, such as a physics engine or a recording. It has a fixed number of slots and no object per particle. Write each particle into its slot, then call upload once a frame: import { packParticleColor, ParticleContainer3D } from '@pixi/3d'; const motes = new ParticleContainer3D({ texture: dot, capacity: 2000, blendMode: 'add' }); const tint = packParticleColor(0x66ff99, 1); view3d.root.addChild(motes); app.ticker.add(() => { for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) motes.writePacked(i, x[i], y[i], z[i], 0.1, 0, tint); motes.upload(); }); writePacked takes the tint and opacity packed into one number by packParticleColor, so particles that share a tint pack it once. setParticleAt takes them unpacked. A slot keeps drawing what you last wrote into it. So when fewer particles are left, write a size of 0 into the slots you stop using, or clear every slot first, as Particle container does when you change its count.

A system builds its shader from shader bits, small pieces of shader code, one for each behaviour. The extraBits option adds your own, which run after the built-in ones. This one sways each particle from side to side: import type { ShaderBit } from '@pixi/3d'; import { ParticleSystem3D } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; const sway = { name: 'sway', bindings: { material: { uSwayAmp: 'f32', uSwayFreq: 'f32' } }, gpu: { vertex: { beforeTransform: /* wgsl */ `position.x += sin(particleAge * material.uSwayFreq) * material.uSwayAmp;` }, }, gl: { vertex: { beforeTransform: /* glsl */ `position.x += sin(particleAge * material.uSwayFreq) * material.uSwayAmp;` }, }, } satisfies ShaderBit; const snow = new ParticleSystem3D({ ...snowOptions, extraBits: [sway] }); snow.uniforms.uSwayAmp = 0.5; snow.uniforms.uSwayFreq = 0.8; Your shader code can read particleAge, in seconds, and particleProgress, which runs from 0 at birth to 1 at death. It can change position, which is in world space unless the system is local. It can also change particleSize, particleRotation and particleColor, which getParticleBit describes. Set the material values your bit declares through uniforms. A vector takes an array, such as [1, 0, 0]. Toon and custom materials shows how to write a bit. Custom particle behaviour swirls sparks with a bit of its own.

destroy stops a system updating, removes it from the scene and frees what it created. It doesn't free the texture you gave it. ParticleContainer3D.destroy lists the flags that do. Removing a system from the scene yourself doesn't stop it updating or emitting.

Post-processing: bloom, a glow around light brighter than white. Interaction: finding the point in the world where a click lands, to spawn particles there. Choosing a node for many objects: when particles fit better than sprites or batched meshes.

A post effect changes the picture a view has drawn. For example, it can add a glow around bright lights, darken creases and corners, or smooth jagged edges. The built-in effects come from @pixi/3d/extras. Add them to the view's passes list, the extra steps the view takes as it draws a frame: import { View3D } from '@pixi/3d'; import { BloomEffect } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; const view3d = new View3D({ autoResize: true, passes: [new BloomEffect({ threshold: 0.7, intensity: 1.8 })], }); A PixiJS filter on the view gets only the picture as the screen will show it. A post effect can also read the scene's depth, the distance to the surface at each pixel, which is how ambient occlusion finds corners. It can also run before tone mapping, the step that turns the scene's light into the colours the screen shows. Before tone mapping, a lamp can still be brighter than white, so bloom can pick it out.

The view copies the array you give it, so pushing to that array later changes nothing. Assign a new array instead, as you would a container's filters: import { SsaoEffect } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; view3d.passes = [new SsaoEffect(), ...view3d.passes]; Each effect runs at a stage. A 'beforeToneMapping' effect works on the scene's light, and an 'afterToneMapping' effect works on the picture as the screen shows it. The view runs the 'beforeToneMapping' effects, then tone mapping, then the 'afterToneMapping' effects, and runs each group in array order. Bloom runs before tone mapping and FXAA after it, so [new FxaaEffect(), new BloomEffect()] still runs FXAA after bloom. Stacking effects shows when order matters. While a 'beforeToneMapping' effect is on, the view draws its scene into a floating-point texture, which can hold light brighter than white. On WebGL2, rendering then throws on a device without the EXT_color_buffer_float extension. How a frame renders shows how to check for it. Turning an effect on and off. Set its enabled to false and the view stops running it. Each change rebuilds the view's render graph, its list of drawing steps, on the next render. It can also recompile the scene's shaders, as When shaders compile lists. That's fine for a settings toggle, but don't toggle it every frame. An effect's other properties, such as intensity or tint, are values its shader reads, so changing them every frame is cheap. An intensity of 0 hides an effect, but the effect still runs. Set enabled = false to save its cost. Antialiasing. An enabled post effect makes the view draw its scene into a texture first, as View3D explains. That texture keeps the canvas's antialias setting, with one exception. If a pass has the scene draw an extra texture the GPU can't average, the scene's edges come out jagged. SsaoEffect with sceneNormals: true on WebGL does this, and SceneOutput lists the formats that cause it. For that view, or for a canvas without antialias, add an FxaaEffect as the last 'afterToneMapping' effect so it smooths the finished picture. Anti-aliasing shows each case. Cleaning up. Replacing the list or destroying the view never destroys the effects in it, since one effect can be in several views. Call destroy on each effect or pass you stop using.

Effect What it does Stage by default BloomEffect Bright parts of the picture glow into their surroundings. 'beforeToneMapping' SsaoEffect Ambient occlusion: darkens creases, corners and the places where objects meet. 'beforeToneMapping' TiltShiftEffect Keeps a band of depth sharp and blurs the rest, so the scene looks like a model. 'beforeToneMapping' MotionBlurEffect Streaks opaque meshes as the camera moves or turns. 'beforeToneMapping' FxaaEffect Smooths jagged edges. 'afterToneMapping' TintEffect Multiplies the picture by a colour, as Container.tint does in 2D. 'afterToneMapping'

By default, BloomEffect works on the scene's light. So at its default threshold, mostly the parts brighter than white glow, such as an emissive glow with a strength above 1, as PBR materials shows. Lower the threshold to make bright but ordinary surfaces glow too. Bloom shows which parts glow at the default threshold.

Use both with a camera in its default perspective mode, not an orthographic one, which draws far things as large as near ones. SsaoEffect.radius is how far around each point the effect looks for surfaces that block light. It's in world units, so set it for the size of your scene. On a phone, create the effect with resolution: 1. That works out the occlusion once per CSS pixel, which is a quarter as many pixels as at the examples' resolution of 2. TiltShiftEffect.focalDepth is a distance straight out from the camera, so set it to about the camera's distance from what should stay sharp. Zooming an OrbitCamera changes that distance. When the subject is at the orbit's target, keep it sharp with orbit.on('change', () => (tiltShift.focalDepth = orbit.distance)). debug paints the sharp band and the blurred zones instead of blurring, which helps you place them.

MotionBlurEffect blurs only by the camera's motion. Turning or moving the camera streaks opaque meshes, but not the view's background. A car driving past a still camera stays sharp. On a camera cut, such as a respawn, call the camera's resetHistory so the jump doesn't smear the first frame of the new shot. Motion blur circles the camera round a ring of clay posts. The posts near its path streak, the logo at the centre of the orbit stays nearly sharp, and a top spinning beside the logo never smears.

FxaaEffect smooths the edges it finds in the finished picture. It can't join up a line thinner than a pixel, since the picture has already broken that line into dashes. In Anti-aliasing, turn the canvas's antialias off and FXAA on to see the smoothed edges and the dashed lines in the example's loupe.

A MeshPass goes in the same passes list. Instead of working on the finished picture, it draws the meshes that join it a second time. An OutlinePass, for example, draws them again as ink outlines. A mesh joins a pass by the pass's name. The usual way is through its material's passes option or enablePass, which join every Mesh3D that shares the material. One mesh can also join through its own enablePass. A BatchedMesh3D slot ignores its material's passes. import { Material3D } from '@pixi/3d'; import { OutlinePass } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; view3d.passes = [...view3d.passes, new OutlinePass({ width: 0.04 })]; const toy = new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xe94f37, passes: { outline: true } }); // every Mesh3D with this material crate.enablePass('outline'); // this mesh only Passes per mesh outlines one of several meshes that share a material. It also takes a mesh out of the 'opaque' pass so only its shadow draws. Toon and custom materials covers outlines, and Debugging covers WireframePass, which draws meshes again as lines. A MeshPass with a camera can draw the scene from a second camera, for a security monitor or a minimap, as Second cameras shows.

A post effect runs a function, effect(uv), once for every pixel of the picture. Subclass PostEffect and give it that function as its fragment, in WGSL for WebGPU and GLSL for WebGL2. The uv argument runs from 0 to 1 across the view, and sampleColor(uv) reads the picture so far. This vignette darkens the picture toward its edges: import { PostEffect } from '@pixi/3d'; import type { EffectFragment, PostEffectOptions } from '@pixi/3d'; import { UniformGroup } from 'pixi.js'; const vignetteFragment: EffectFragment = { gpu: /* wgsl */ ` fn effect(uv: vec2<f32>) -> vec4<f32> { let color = sampleColor(uv); let edge = smoothstep(0.3, 0.8, distance(uv, vec2<f32>(0.5))); return vec4<f32>(color.rgb * (1.0 - edge * fx.uStrength), color.a); } `, gl: /* glsl */ ` vec4 effect(vec2 uv) { vec4 color = sampleColor(uv); float edge = smoothstep(0.3, 0.8, distance(uv, vec2(0.5))); return vec4(color.rgb * (1.0 - edge * uStrength), color.a); } `, }; class MyVignetteEffect extends PostEffect { protected override readonly uniforms = new UniformGroup({ uStrength: { value: 0.6, type: 'f32' } }); protected readonly fragment = vignetteFragment; constructor(options: PostEffectOptions = {}) { super({ stage: 'afterToneMapping', ...options }); } public get strength(): number { return this.uniforms.uniforms.uStrength as number; } public set strength(value: number) { this.uniforms.uniforms.uStrength = value; } } view3d.passes = [new MyVignetteEffect()]; The uniforms are the effect's settings. The shader reads them as fx.<name> in WGSL and as plain <name> in GLSL. PixiJS uploads their values every frame, so a setter only has to write the value. An effect runs at 'beforeToneMapping' unless its constructor passes another stage to super. The vignette darkens the picture as the screen shows it, so it passes 'afterToneMapping'. It spreads options after the stage, so one instance can still pick its own stage. The fragment can also call helpers. sampleDepth(uv) and viewPos(uv) read the scene's depth, and texel() gives the size of one pixel in uv units. EffectFragment lists them all. Which way uv.y runs on screen differs between WebGL and WebGPU, so don't make an effect depend on it. An effect that needs more than one drawing step, as bloom does, overrides build instead. Custom render passes shows how, and Custom effect runs one beside a vignette.
Custom render passes: effects in several steps, and mesh passes with a shader of your own. How a frame renders: where each stage runs in a frame. Performance: keeping post effects few on phones.

A view draws each frame as a list of passes called its render graph. Each pass draws one part of the picture, such as the shadows, the opaque meshes or one step of an effect. Each item in view3d.passes is a Pass3D. When the view builds its graph, each enabled item adds its own passes at its stage, the point in the frame where they run. Post-processing covers the built-in items and effects made of one shader.

A MeshPass draws every mesh that joins it a second time, with a shader of its own. Meshes join it by its name, as Mesh passes shows. OutlinePass is a mesh pass named 'outline'. It draws each mesh again in one flat colour, as a shell pushed out along its normals, the directions its surface faces. OutlinePass draws black ink outlines on the meshes that join 'outline'. A white rim around the mesh under the pointer takes a second pass. A second OutlinePass makes the view throw, since it's also named 'outline'. Give a MeshPass a name of its own instead: import { MeshPass, stateFor3D } from '@pixi/3d'; import { OutlinePass, solidMeshDescriptor } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; // Culls the front faces instead of the back, as OutlinePass does, so the mesh hides all of the shell but a rim const shell = stateFor3D(); shell.clockwiseFrontFace = true; view3d.passes = [ new OutlinePass(), new MeshPass({ name: 'highlight', descriptor: { shaderDescriptor: solidMeshDescriptor({ color: 0xffffff, extrude: 0.06 }), state: shell }, }), ]; mesh.eventMode = 'static'; mesh.onpointerenter = () => mesh.enablePass('highlight'); mesh.onpointerleave = () => mesh.disablePass('highlight'); A name of your own needs a shader. It comes from the pass's descriptor, or from a material's entry for that name in its passes option. solidMeshDescriptor draws in one flat colour, which you set when you create it and can't change later. The first hover can stall while the pass's shader compiles, as When shaders compile describes. Give the pass a state too. Without one, the pass uses the material's state. A pushed-out shell then covers the whole mesh, and a second draw of an opaque mesh with no extrude lands exactly on the first. The depth test keeps only what's nearer than what's already there, so it rejects that draw. Cull the front faces of a shell, as above. For a draw with no extrude, turn depthTest off so it draws over what's already there. Names are limited. All views on the page share a limited number of name slots, and a name past the last slot joins nothing. Use a few fixed names rather than one per object. RenderPassBit has the details.

Writing an effect shows an effect made of one function. An effect that needs several steps overrides build and adds a FullscreenPass for each step. A FullscreenPass draws an effect(uv) function once over the whole picture. It samples the textures in its reads and draws into its writes. A blur costs less in two steps, across and then down. That's five samples per pixel in each step, ten in all, rather than twenty-five in a single step: import { FullscreenPass, PostEffect } from '@pixi/3d'; import type { EffectFragment, EffectIO, RenderGraph } from '@pixi/3d'; // Averages five pixels in a line, `d` apart function blurFragment(gpuStep: string, glStep: string): EffectFragment { const sum = 'sampleColor(uv - 2.0 * d) + sampleColor(uv - d) + sampleColor(uv) + sampleColor(uv + d) + sampleColor(uv + 2.0 * d)'; return { gpu: `fn effect(uv: vec2<f32>) -> vec4<f32> { let d = ${gpuStep}; return (${sum}) / 5.0; }`, gl: `vec4 effect(vec2 uv) { vec2 d = ${glStep}; return (${sum}) / 5.0; }`, }; } const blurAcross = blurFragment('vec2<f32>(inputTexel().x, 0.0)', 'vec2(inputTexel().x, 0.0)'); const blurDown = blurFragment('vec2<f32>(0.0, inputTexel().y)', 'vec2(0.0, inputTexel().y)'); class MyBlurEffect extends PostEffect { public override build(graph: RenderGraph, io: EffectIO): void { const across = graph.createColor(); graph.addPass( new FullscreenPass({ renderer: io.renderer, fragment: blurAcross, reads: { color: io.input }, writes: across }), ); graph.addPass( new FullscreenPass({ renderer: io.renderer, fragment: blurDown, reads: { color: across }, writes: io.output }), ); } } view3d.passes = [new MyBlurEffect()]; io.input is the picture so far, and the last step draws into io.output. graph.createColor() makes a texture the size of the scene for the steps in between. It lasts one frame, so it doesn't hold last frame's result. inputTexel() is the size of one pixel of the step's input in uv units. EffectFragment lists the other helpers.

An effect can also read a scene output, an extra texture that the scene draw writes beside its colour. normalOutput, for example, holds each surface's normal. An item that lists an output in its requiredOutputs makes the scene write it, and reads it in build with RenderGraph.getSceneOutput. Some formats cost the scene its antialiasing, including normalOutput's format on WebGL, as The passes list says. Like a texture from createColor, an output lasts only for the frame. ExtractPass copies one into a texture you keep, which a sprite can show: import { ExtractPass, normalOutput } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; import { Sprite } from 'pixi.js'; const normals = new ExtractPass({ output: normalOutput }); view3d.passes = [normals]; app.stage.addChild(new Sprite(normals.texture)); Scene outputs defines two outputs of its own, each surface's base colour and its distance from the camera. It shows them beside normalOutput in three cards. Its see-through sphere is blended, so it doesn't show in any of them. To keep a result of your own past the frame, write it into a texture you own. Add that texture to the graph with graph.importColor, which takes a function that returns it, such as () => myTexture. The graph never clears it. A FullscreenPass can't sample an imported texture yet, and trying throws. Show or read it outside the graph instead, the way a sprite shows ExtractPass's texture.
documents.s: Scene outputs and textures you keep

documents.t: To add passes other than a MeshPass or a PostEffect, subclass Pass3D and add them in its build at one of the three scene stages, as A sky in the feed does. graph.addPass takes either a pass, such as a FullscreenPass, or a plain object with a name, a setup and a render. These rules hold for both: A pass runs only when something needs what it writes. Its setup runs once, when you add it, and uses the PassBuilder to declare which textures it reads and writes. Each frame, the graph runs the pass only when a later pass that runs reads what it writes, or when the pass writes the view's own target, a texture you imported or a camera's render texture. The view's own target is usually the screen. A pass that declares nothing never runs. A pass that only reads, such as a readback to the CPU, calls b.sideEffect() in setup so it runs anyway. Passes run in the order you add them. What they declare doesn't reorder them, so a pass that reads a texture sees only what earlier passes wrote. A pass's condition can skip it each frame. The graph calls prepare and then render on each pass that runs. GraphRenderPass says when each of these methods runs, and RenderGraph.getTexture covers a pass that binds a texture itself. A pass that draws no meshes takes bit: RenderPassBit.NONE. Any number of passes with that bit can share a view. Make handles in build or setup, never in a constructor. A handle from createColor or the PassBuilder stands for a texture the graph supplies each frame. It works only in the graph that made it. Each rebuild starts a new graph and calls each enabled item's build again. The view rebuilds after changes such as assigning view3d.passes or flipping a pass's enabled. The graph destroys the passes that build added. It does this when the view replaces the graph or the view is destroyed. You destroy the item itself, as The passes list says, so free anything it made outside the graph in an override of destroy.

The graph option replaces the view's graph with one that your function builds. The view calls that function on the first render and again on each rebuild. To add passes that no stage can place, start from createDefaultGraph3D and add your passes to its graph. To draw something else entirely, build a bare RenderGraph, which runs only the passes you add. The graph below draws the opaque meshes in white into a texture. That makes a silhouette mask with no shadows, sky or lighting, and a sprite shows it: import { Camera3D, ForwardRenderPass, RenderGraph, View3D } from '@pixi/3d'; import { solidMeshDescriptor } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; import { RenderTexture, Sprite } from 'pixi.js'; const mask = RenderTexture.create({ width: 384, height: 384 }); const maskCamera = new Camera3D({ renderTexture: mask }); maskCamera.position.set(0, 1.5, 7); maskCamera.lookAt({ x: 0, y: 0.3, z: 0 }); const view3d = new View3D({ width: 384, height: 384, graph: (renderer, options) => { const graph = new RenderGraph({ globalTextureBindings: options.globalTextureBindings, defaultColor: (session) => session.defaultTarget.colorTexture, defaultDepth: (session) => session.defaultTarget.depthStencilTexture!, }); graph.addPass( new ForwardRenderPass({ renderer, name: 'opaque', sort: 'key', camera: maskCamera, descriptor: { shaderDescriptor: solidMeshDescriptor({ color: 0xffffff }) }, }), ); return graph; }, }); view3d.root.addChild(maskCamera); app.stage.addChild(view3d, new Sprite(mask)); The ForwardRenderPass is named 'opaque', so it draws the meshes whose materials put them in the opaque pass. It uses the shader in its descriptor rather than the materials' own shaders. It draws from the mask's camera, so place and move that camera. No pass here draws from view3d.camera, so moving it changes nothing. The mask's camera has a render texture, so the view puts nothing on screen and the sprite shows the texture instead. Give a pass's descriptor a whole shader descriptor, such as the one solidMeshDescriptor returns, because a pass has no default template. A template is the shader source that shader bits fill in, and shader bits are small pieces of shader code. Toon and custom materials covers writing shader bits.

Post-processing: the built-in effects and mesh passes. How a frame renders: where each stage runs in a frame. Debugging: record frames to see the passes the view built, which ones it skipped, and what each read and wrote.

A 3D scene is a tree of nodes under a view's root. Every node is a Container3D, the 3D counterpart of a 2D Container. So you move, turn, scale and group every kind of node the same way, as Scene graph and transforms shows.

Container3D draws nothing. It groups nodes so they move together. Mesh3D draws a shape, its Geometry3D, with a material that decides how the surface looks. See Meshes. Model3D turns a glTF file into nodes: meshes, lights, cameras and empty containers. glTF is the 3D model format PixiJS 3D loads. When the file has animations, the model also gets an animation player. See Loading models. Sprite3D draws a texture on a flat card. The card takes its size from the texture and, by default, turns to face the camera. See Sprite3D. BatchedMesh3D draws many meshes from one node. Each mesh is a slot that holds a geometry, a material and a matrix that places it. A slot has no node of its own. See Batched meshes. ParticleContainer3D draws up to a fixed number of flat cards in one draw call, at the positions your code writes. ParticleSystem3D, from @pixi/3d/extras, is a particle container that emits and moves its particles on its own. See Particles. Camera3D is the point of view the scene is drawn from. A view comes with one, at view3d.camera. See Cameras. AmbientLight, DirectionalLight, PointLight and SpotLight light the meshes whose material reacts to light, such as Material3D. See Lights. Light from the surroundings, such as a sky, isn't a node. It comes from the view's environment; see Environment.

A 3D node isn't a 2D Container, so it can't go on app.stage. The View3D goes on the stage, and every 3D node goes under view3d.root, at any depth. A node that isn't under a view's root draws nothing and lights nothing. 2D content, such as a Text, can't go under the root either. Draw it onto a 3D surface with a ContainerTexture instead, as Rendering 2D into 3D shows. Or keep it on the stage and pin it over a 3D point with worldToScreen. The view finds every mesh and light wherever it sits in the tree, so a light can have a mesh as a child, and a mesh can have a light. Here a point light has a glowing bulb as its child, so the bulb moves with it: import { Material3D, Mesh3D, PointLight, SphereGeometry } from '@pixi/3d'; const color = 0xff2e7e; const light = new PointLight({ color, intensity: 8, range: 6 }); // An emissive material glows in its own colour, whatever light reaches it const bulb = new Mesh3D({ geometry: new SphereGeometry({ radius: 0.09 }), material: new Material3D({ baseColor: 0x000000, emissive: { color, strength: 4 } }), castShadow: false, // a glowing bulb shouldn't cast a shadow }); light.addChild(bulb); view3d.root.addChild(light); app.ticker.add(() => { const time = performance.now() / 1000; light.position.set(Math.cos(time) * 2.6, 1.2, Math.sin(time) * 2.6); // the bulb moves with the light }); Hiding the light with visible turns it off and hides the bulb too. Scene graph and transforms covers the rest, including why, unlike in 2D, the order of children doesn't decide what covers what.

You have Use Objects you place, click and animate one by one Mesh3D Copies of a loaded model that each animate on their own Several Model3Ds built from one loaded file Up to a few thousand cards that face the camera and mostly stay put, such as trees Sprite3D Thousands of copies of a mesh, such as trees, rocks, stars or bullets BatchedMesh3D Fire, smoke, sparks or snow that emit, move and fade on their own ParticleSystem3D Thousands of cards that your own code moves every frame ParticleContainer3D For a glTF file, Assets.load returns a Scene3DSource. Models built from one source share its geometry, materials and textures, as Loading models explains. Each model has its own nodes and, when the file has animations, its own AnimationPlayer. Each mesh and each sprite, including the meshes inside a model, is a scene node. A mesh or sprite that moves, or sits under a node that moves, costs CPU time on every frame it moves, because the view works out its place in the world again. The view also sorts the meshes and sprites that blend with what's behind them back to front every frame, whether they move or not. A sprite that makes its own material blends by default; see alphaMode. Meshes that don't move and share their draw calls cost the CPU little each frame. Performance says what lets them share. Their number still counts, because each node takes memory and time to build. Where the view culls on the CPU, as it does by default under WebGL2, it works out each frame which meshes the camera can't see and skips them. That work grows with the number of meshes. So put scenery, such as a forest's trees and rocks, in BatchedMesh3D slots. A few thousand meshes that never move are fine, but for tens of thousands, use slots. A batched mesh and a particle container have no node per copy, so moving a copy means writing into an array. Unlike pixi's 2D ParticleContainer, a ParticleContainer3D has no object per particle. You write each card by its index with writePacked, then call upload once a frame, as Driving particles yourself shows. You set its capacity when you create it and can't change it later. Writing past it throws, so build a bigger container when your particles outgrow it.
documents.s: Choosing a node for many objects

documents.t: Meshes: building a mesh from a geometry and a material, and sharing and swapping them. Cameras and Lights: seeing and lighting a scene. Performance: draw calls, culling and a checklist for phones.

A BatchedMesh3D draws many meshes from one scene node. Each mesh is a slot: a geometry, a material and a matrix that places it, with no Mesh3D of its own. Choosing a node for many objects says when to pick it over meshes, sprites or particles. A slot is rigid. It can't bend with bones or morph targets, so keep animated characters as Model3Ds. BatchedMesh3D draws a ring of up to 100,000 clay shapes from one batch.

You set the number of slots when you create the batch, and it can't change later. Make it enough for the most meshes you'll show at once. The renderer draws each frame in steps called passes, such as shadows and then solid meshes. Give each slot a geometry, a material and a matrix, and put it in the passes that draw it: import { BatchedMesh3D, ConeGeometry, Material3D, Matrix4, Quaternion, RenderPassBit, Vector3 } from '@pixi/3d'; const COUNT = 2000; const forest = new BatchedMesh3D({ size: COUNT }); const cone = new ConeGeometry({ radius: 0.6, height: 2, radialSegments: 8 }); // few sides, since it draws 2,000 times const pine = new Material3D({ baseColor: 0x2f6b3a, roughness: 0.9 }); const matrix = new Matrix4(); const position = new Vector3(); const rotation = new Quaternion(); const scale = new Vector3(); for (let i = 0; i < COUNT; i++) { const size = 0.7 + Math.random() * 0.6; // A tree somewhere in a 200 x 200 square, standing on the ground, turned at random position.set((Math.random() - 0.5) * 200, size, (Math.random() - 0.5) * 200); rotation.setFromAxisAngle({ x: 0, y: 1, z: 0 }, Math.random() * Math.PI * 2); scale.set(size); forest.setGeometryAt(i, cone); forest.setMaterialAt(i, pine); forest.setMatrixAt(i, matrix.compose(position, rotation, scale)); forest.setPassesAt(i, RenderPassBit.OPAQUE | RenderPassBit.SHADOW); } view3d.root.addChild(forest); A slot doesn't take its passes from its material, as a mesh does. Give it RenderPassBit flags with setPassesAt to match the material, such as OPAQUE for an alphaMode of 'opaque' or 'mask' and TRANSPARENT for 'blend'. A Material3D with transmission takes TRANSMISSION instead. Add SHADOW to cast shadows. No flag puts a slot in a mesh pass, such as an outline, so a slot can't have one. A slot in a pass needs a geometry and a material, even while it's hidden. Spare slots that are in no pass can stay empty. A new slot's matrix is all zeros, so it draws nothing until you set one. The matrix places the slot relative to the BatchedMesh3D. compose builds one from a position, a rotation and a scale. An object made of parts, such as a trunk and a crown, takes a slot per part, so count parts when you size the batch. A part's matrix is the object's matrix times the part's offset on the object. tree.multiply(offset, part) writes it into part, and the part turns and scales with the tree. Moving, turning or hiding the BatchedMesh3D does the same to every slot at once. On WebGPU, though, 'blend' slots can overlap in the wrong order once the batch or a parent moves, turns or scales. Keep a batch of them at the origin, unturned and unscaled, and place the slots with their matrices. Slots can mix geometries and materials, and they share draw calls by the same rules as meshes. What makes a draw call lists those rules. A slot has no tint like a 2D sprite's, and changing a material changes every slot that uses it. To recolour one slot, give it another material with setMaterialAt, which on WebGPU costs a draw call per material. Or give it a value of your own, which keeps one draw call.

setMatrixAt copies a matrix into the slot and allocates nothing, so you can call it for every slot every frame. To move thousands of slots a frame, skip the copy and write into the batch's own array, matrices. Slot i's matrix is the 16 numbers starting at offset + i * stride, stored column by column. Numbers 12, 13 and 14 hold its position, and numbers 0 to 2, 4 to 6 and 8 to 10 hold its rotation and scale. After writing, call update() once, or the GPU may never see what you wrote. This code swirls a galaxy of slots round the origin, with the inner ones faster: app.ticker.add((ticker) => { time += ticker.deltaMS / 1000; const { data, stride, offset } = galaxy.matrices; for (let i = 0, o = offset; i < galaxy.size; i++, o += stride) { const angle = angles[i] - (time * 3) / (radii[i] + 2); // inner spheres orbit faster data[o + 12] = Math.cos(angle) * radii[i]; data[o + 14] = Math.sin(angle) * radii[i]; } galaxy.matrices.update(); }); Set each slot's whole matrix once, with setMatrixAt or through matrices, before you write only the numbers that move. Write only a slot's 16 numbers. The numbers after them hold engine data. BatchedMesh3D lifts slots this way, then calls update(first, count) for just the slots it wrote.

setVisibleAt hides or shows a slot, as visible does for a mesh. A hidden slot draws nothing, not even its shadow. It keeps its geometry, material, matrix and passes, so showing it again rebuilds nothing. That makes hiding and showing the way to spawn and despawn. Every slot starts visible, so hide the spares first: const bullets = new BatchedMesh3D({ size: 200, parent: view3d.root }); for (let i = 0; i < bullets.size; i++) { bullets.setGeometryAt(i, bulletGeometry); bullets.setMaterialAt(i, bulletMaterial); bullets.setPassesAt(i, RenderPassBit.OPAQUE); bullets.setVisibleAt(i, false); // a spare until fire() uses it } function fire(muzzle: Matrix4): void { for (let i = 0; i < bullets.size; i++) { if (bullets.getVisibleAt(i)) continue; // in flight bullets.setMatrixAt(i, muzzle); bullets.setVisibleAt(i, true); return; } } Hidden 'blend' slots still cost a sort every frame. setVisibleAt says when to take a spare out of its pass with setPassesAt(i, 0) instead.

setMaterialAt and setGeometryAt give a slot a new material or geometry. The slot keeps its passes, so when the new material needs other passes, such as a 'blend' material replacing an 'opaque' one, call setPassesAt too. When you edit a material that slots already use, changes to values such as baseColor show up on their own. After a texture swap, though, call invalidate for each slot that uses the material, or those slots keep the old texture. invalidate lists the other changes that need it. leaves.textures.baseColor = autumnLeaves; for (const i of leafSlots) trees.invalidate(i); A slot's billboardMode and receiveShadow are in items, and changing either also needs invalidate.

For a value that changes per slot, such as a tint that fades every frame, declare a field with the instanceData option. Read it as instance.<name> in a shader bit, a piece of shader code you add to the material with extraBits. Adding your own shader code explains bits. import { BatchedMesh3D, Material3D } from '@pixi/3d'; import type { ShaderBit } from '@pixi/3d'; const tintBit: ShaderBit = { name: 'slotTint', bindings: { instance: { tint: 'vec4<f32>' } }, gpu: { fragment: { material: 'albedo *= instance.tint.rgb;' } }, gl: { fragment: { material: 'albedo *= instance.tint.rgb;' } }, }; const boxes = new BatchedMesh3D({ size: 1000, instanceData: { tint: { value: [1, 1, 1, 1], type: 'vec4<f32>' } } }); const paint = new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xffffff, extraBits: [tintBit] }); // Fill the slots with paint, as the forest above does, then: boxes.setInstanceDataAt(0, 'tint', 1, 0.2, 0.2, 1); // slot 0 turns red setInstanceDataAt writes one slot. To change many slots a frame, write into the instanceData array, which works like matrices and has its own update().

A slot with PlaneGeometry.spriteQuad and a billboardMode is a card that turns to face the camera. The matrix's x and y scale set the card's width and height: import { Matrix4, PlaneGeometry, RenderPassBit } from '@pixi/3d'; const card = new Matrix4(); grass.setGeometryAt(i, PlaneGeometry.spriteQuad); grass.setMaterialAt(i, bladeMaterial); // 0.4 wide and 0.8 tall, standing on the ground grass.setMatrixAt(i, card.makeScale(0.4, 0.8, 1).setPosition({ x, y: 0.4, z })); grass.setPassesAt(i, RenderPassBit.OPAQUE); // no SHADOW, since a light draws a card's shadow from the unturned card grass.items[i].billboardMode = 'cylindrical'; // turns about its upright axis only, so it stays standing grass.invalidate(i);

Culling skips drawing what's outside the camera's view. A batch uses its own cull setting, not the view's cull. It's 'off' by default, so every slot in a pass draws, on screen or not. Turn it on for a large batch that spreads well beyond the view, such as scenery across a whole map: const forest = new BatchedMesh3D({ size: 10_000, cull: 'gpu' }); Once culling is on, the batch tests its slots every frame, and again for each shadow map that redraws. Where the test runs on the CPU, as under WebGL2, that work grows with the slot count. On the GPU, it costs the CPU almost nothing. With the whole batch in view, the test still runs but culls nothing. So for a camera that zooms out to see all of it, culling saves work only while zoomed in. CullMode says when to use each mode.

A slot in the SHADOW pass counts as a shadow caster, even while it's hidden. A directional light's shadow box is the part of the world its shadows cover. By default, the light refits that box only while the scene has few casters, so with a large batch it fits the box once and keeps it. One box over the scene explains this. After you move or spawn slots outside the box, call fitShadowBounds, or set your own box with shadow.bounds.

destroy frees the batch's own buffers. It leaves the slots' geometries and materials alone, since they're often shared, unless you pass geometry or material, or true to set every flag. With those flags, it destroys each geometry or material once, however many slots use it: forest.destroy({ geometry: true, material: true }); Use unload for a batch you'll show again later. Unloading says what it frees.

Performance: what puts meshes in one draw call, and keeping a scene fast on phones. Sprite3D: cards with a sprite's API, for hundreds to a few thousand cards. Particles: effects that emit, move and fade on their own.

A Camera3D is the point of view a View3D draws its scene from. Every view comes with one, at view3d.camera, and it sits under view3d.root with the rest of the scene. A camera is a Container3D, so you move, turn and parent it like any other node. Moving view3d.root, the way you'd scroll a 2D world container, doesn't scroll the picture. The camera moves with the root, so meshes stay where they were on screen. Particles don't move with the root by default, so they slide out of place. Scaling the root doesn't zoom in either. Move the camera, or set its zoom, instead.

The camera starts at the origin, which is also where new meshes start, so move it away from them first. It looks along its own -Z axis, so with no rotation it looks into the screen. lookAt turns it to face a point in world space, the coordinates of the scene as a whole: view3d.camera.position.set(0, 2, 6); // up, and back toward the viewer view3d.camera.lookAt({ x: 0, y: 0.5, z: 0 }); lookAt turns the camera once. When the camera or the point moves, call it again each frame, after the move. Scene graph and transforms covers the axes, and how lookAt and rotation interact on one node. To steer the camera with the mouse, touch or keys, use a controller from Camera controls. Add the camera under another node and it moves and turns with that node. If you remove the camera or any node above it from the view, or hide one of them, the view throws an error the next time it draws. So when a player carries the camera, put the player's model and the camera side by side in a plain Container3D. Then you can hide or scale the model without hiding or scaling the camera.

A camera starts in perspective mode, where distant things look smaller. fov is the vertical field of view, the angle in degrees from the bottom to the top of what the camera sees. The picture's shape sets the horizontal field of view. A portrait phone sees less to each side than a landscape monitor, so a scene that fits the monitor loses its sides on the phone. Framing a model shows how to back the camera off far enough for either shape. zoom magnifies on top of fov. At a zoom of 2, the scene looks twice as large. The view reads every camera setting each time it draws, so you can change or animate them at any time.

A camera draws only what lies between its near and far distances in front of it. It doesn't draw anything closer than near, so a camera that comes too close to a model cuts a hole in it. Keep near as large as the scene allows. The depth buffer stores how far away each pixel is, and its precision is limited. With a tiny near, distant surfaces that sit close together store the same depth and flicker through each other. Raising near fixes that. Lowering far barely helps. view3d.camera.near = 0.5; // just short of the closest the camera gets to anything it shows view3d.camera.far = 300; // just past the farthest thing it shows

Set mode to 'orthographic' and nothing shrinks with distance, which suits isometric games, maps and editors. orthographicSize is half the width the camera sees, in world units. The picture's shape sets the height, so the width always fits, and a portrait phone sees more above and below. const camera = view3d.camera; camera.mode = 'orthographic'; camera.orthographicSize = 10; // 20 units across camera.position.set(20, 20, 20); camera.lookAt({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 }); // looks down the diagonal for an isometric view Moving an orthographic camera closer doesn't make anything bigger. Shrink orthographicSize instead, or raise zoom, which magnifies here too. The camera still draws only between near and far, so keep the whole scene in front of it. With an orthographic camera, leave the view's background null and give the app a background colour instead.

Assign another camera to view3d.camera to draw from it. If that camera has no parent, the view adds it under view3d.root. If it already has a parent, it must be in this view's scene when you assign it, or the assignment throws an error. A glTF file, the model format PixiJS 3D loads, can bring its own cameras, and model.cameras lists them. They sit inside the model, so add the model to the view first: import { Model3D } from '@pixi/3d'; const model = new Model3D({ source }); const ownCamera = view3d.camera; view3d.root.addChild(model); if (model.cameras.length > 0) view3d.camera = model.cameras[0]; // Later, switch back to the view's own camera view3d.camera = ownCamera; The previous camera stays in the scene as it was, so assigning it again switches back. A controller drives whichever camera the view has, so an OrbitCamera takes over the new camera on its next update. While the view draws from another camera, turn off the controller's enabled so input leaves the camera alone. Also stop its updates, either by turning off autoUpdate or by skipping your own update() calls. Undo both when you switch back. If you destroy the view's camera, or the model it came from, assign another camera before the view next draws, or that draw throws an error.

View3D.from builds a view around a loaded glTF file and gives it a camera, as Loading models covers. To frame a model in a view of your own, put a Sphere around it and move the camera back until the whole sphere is in view. getLocalBounds ignores the position, rotation and scale of the model and its parents. So the snippet applies getGlobalTransform to move the sphere to where the model is in the world: import { Sphere } from '@pixi/3d'; const camera = view3d.camera; const sphere = new Sphere().setFromBox(model.getLocalBounds()).applyMatrix4(model.getGlobalTransform()); const { center, radius } = sphere; // Half the narrower field of view, which is the horizontal one on a portrait screen and the vertical one otherwise const aspect = app.screen.width / app.screen.height; const halfFov = Math.atan(Math.tan((camera.fov * Math.PI) / 360) * Math.min(1, aspect)); const distance = radius / Math.sin(halfFov); // Any direction works at that distance. This one looks down from about 30 degrees. camera.position.set(center.x, center.y + distance * 0.5, center.z + distance * 0.87); camera.lookAt(center); // Models come in any size, so near and far scale with the distance camera.near = distance / 100; camera.far = distance * 100; app.screen matches the view's shape when the view fills the screen. For a view of a set size, use the view's width and height. With an OrbitCamera, copy center into its target instead of calling lookAt. Set its minDistance and maxDistance from the model too, such as radius and distance * 5. The controller keeps the camera between those two distances, so limits sized for another scene pull it in or push it out.

Camera controls: orbit and first-person controllers. Second cameras: the scene from a second camera, drawn into a texture for a monitor or a portal. View3D and 2D content: worldToScreen and screenToRay, which convert between the screen and the scene through the view's camera.

@pixi/3d/extras has two controllers that move view3d.camera for you. OrbitCamera turns it around a point as the user drags, for model viewers and strategy maps. FPSCamera turns it with the mouse or a finger and moves it with the keys, for walking through a scene. A controller owns the camera's rotation, so steer the camera through the controller rather than with the camera's lookAt. The orbit camera turns the camera to face its target on every update. The first-person camera sets the rotation from its yaw and pitch. Yaw is how far it has turned left or right, and pitch is how far it has tilted up or down.

Place the camera, then give the controller the view and the point to orbit: import { OrbitCamera } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; view3d.camera.position.set(0, 2, 6); const orbit = new OrbitCamera({ view: view3d, target: { x: 0, y: 1, z: 0 }, enableDamping: true, minDistance: 2, maxDistance: 12, maxPolarAngle: Math.PI * 0.48, }); The OrbitCamera reference lists its mouse and touch gestures, and mouseButtons and touches reassign them. The controller starts from wherever the camera is, so move the camera away from the target first. A new camera sits at the origin, which is also the default target, so it has no distance to turn or zoom through. When a model file has no camera, View3D.from places a new one facing the middle of the model. But the orbit camera's target still starts at the origin, so the controller turns the camera to face the origin, and the top of a tall model standing there goes off screen. Pass the model's centre as the target: const orbit = new OrbitCamera({ view: view3d, target: view3d.root.getLocalBounds().getCenter() }); To drag an object without turning the camera, stop the event's propagation, as Dragging shows. A drag that orbits the camera and ends on the model it started on still fires pointertap on that model. Clicks, hover and cursors shows how to tell a tap from a drag. PixiJS listens for wheel events passively, so the browser still acts on them. In a page that scrolls, the wheel scrolls the page as well as zooming the camera, and in Chrome a trackpad pinch zooms the whole page. A wheel listener of your own on the canvas stops both, and the camera still zooms: app.canvas.addEventListener('wheel', (e) => e.preventDefault(), { passive: false });

With enableDamping on, turning and panning keep going for a moment after the pointer stops moving, then ease to a stop. Zooming still happens at once. autoRotate turns the camera around the target by itself, for a turntable view, and pauses while the user drags.

minDistance and maxDistance set how close to the target the camera can get and how far from it, so size them to the model. An orthographic camera draws far things as large as near ones. It zooms by changing its zoom instead, between minZoom and maxZoom. maxPolarAngle limits how low the camera goes. The polar angle is 0 straight above the target and π/2 level with it. A little under π/2 keeps the camera above the target's height, and so above a floor the target sits on.

zoomToCursor makes the wheel zoom toward the point under the pointer, and a pinch zoom toward the point between the fingers. With screenSpacePanning off, a pan moves the target across the ground at the target's own height instead of across the screen. Set the left button and one finger to pan as well, and these two options make a map or strategy-game camera: view3d.camera.position.set(0, 10, 10); const orbit = new OrbitCamera({ view: view3d, zoomToCursor: true, screenSpacePanning: false, mouseButtons: { left: 'pan', right: 'rotate' }, touches: { one: 'pan', two: 'zoom-rotate' }, minDistance: 4, maxDistance: 40, maxPolarAngle: Math.PI / 3, }); note For content built with Z as its up axis rather than Y, such as terrain from map data, keep up at its default, +Y. Then stand the content upright in a Container3D with rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2.

rotate, pan and zoom move the camera the way a gesture does. Use them for keyboard shortcuts or buttons. Damping eases a turn or a pan from these calls the same way it eases a gesture. // Swing round and up from the starting view, and step back a little orbit.rotate(0.7, 0.35); orbit.zoom(0.8); To jump to a new view, set the camera's position and the target together. The controller picks up both on its next update, within its limits. With damping on, a turn or pan that is still easing to a stop when you jump carries on from the new view. Framing a model shows how far back to put the camera.

import { FPSCamera } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; const walker = new FPSCamera({ view: view3d, position: { x: 0, y: 1.7, z: 9 }, pointerLock: true, }); The First-person camera example walks through a clay maze and has an on-screen joystick for touch. Dragging looks around, the WASD or arrow keys walk, and Space and Shift move the camera up and down. With pointerLock on, a mouse press captures the pointer instead of starting a drag. Moving the mouse then looks around until the user presses Escape. Touch still looks by dragging. The example folds its settings pane away while the pointer is captured, using the controller's lock and unlock events. A page in a sandboxed iframe without allow-pointer-lock can't capture the pointer. With pointerLock on, the mouse then can't look around at all. If the document fires pointerlockerror before any capture has worked, turn pointerLock off. The camera starts facing -Z, into the screen, whatever rotation it had before, unless you pass a yaw and pitch. Turn the camera by changing those two. Unlike a 2D rotation, a positive yaw turns it left. W walks the way the camera looks, pitch included, so walking while looking down sinks the camera through the floor. The controller has no gravity or walls. Updating each frame shows how to hold the camera at eye height. The controller reads keys from window, so typing W into a text field on the page walks too. Turn keyboard off while a field has focus.
