In the floating-shapes tutorial, a container moves each shape around while the mesh inside it spins: import { Container3D, Mesh3D } from '@pixi/3d'; const float = new Container3D(); const mesh = new Mesh3D({ geometry, material }); float.addChild(mesh); view3d.root.addChild(float); app.ticker.add((ticker) => { float.position.y = Math.sin(ticker.lastTime / 1000) * 0.25; // bob up and down mesh.rotation.y += 0.5 * (ticker.deltaMS / 1000); // spin in place }); As with 2D's ContainerOptions, every node's constructor takes Container3DOptions, such as position, rotation and label, on top of its own options. The child methods and events match a 2D Container's, such as addChild, removeFromParent and the added event. Container3DEvents lists the events. Unlike 2D, the order of children doesn't decide what covers what. A nearer solid surface hides a farther one. getChildByLabel finds a node by its label. A loaded model labels each node with its name in the file, as Loading models covers. That lets you find a part by name, such as a car's wheel: const car = new Model3D({ source }); const wheel = car.getChildByLabel('wheel-front-left', true); // true searches the whole subtree A skinned model, such as a character, has a mesh that bends with a skeleton. A bone becomes a node only when the file puts a mesh under it, so getChildByLabel doesn't find the others. Every bone is in a Skeleton on the model, and Animation shows how to find one by name and pose it.

These methods convert between a node's own space and world space: getGlobalPosition returns a node's position in world space. toGlobal converts a point from the node's own space to world space. toLocal converts a point in world space, or in another node's space, into the node's own space. In Parents and children, turning an empty orbit node carries a planet round the sun. The planet's position never changes, and getGlobalPosition returns where the orbit has moved it: import { Vector3 } from '@pixi/3d'; orbit.addChild(planet); planet.position.x = 2.5; // 2.5 units out from the orbit's centre const world = new Vector3(); app.ticker.add((ticker) => { orbit.rotation.y += 0.45 * (ticker.deltaMS / 1000); planet.getGlobalPosition(world); // writes into world, so it allocates nothing each frame }); To place 2D content over a 3D node, pass its world position to worldToScreen, which View3D and 2D content covers.

addChild keeps a node's local position, rotation and scale, so a node jumps when its new parent sits somewhere else. reparentChild moves it under the new parent and changes its local transform so it stays where it was in the world: hand.reparentChild(sword); // the sword stays put, and from now on follows the hand
documents.s: Moving a node to a new parent

documents.t: Changing a position, rotation or scale only marks the node as changed. worldTransform holds what the view worked out the last time it drew, normally once a frame, so it can be out of date: after a change you made since the view last drew, while the node or one of its parents is hidden, for a node that isn't under a view's root. getGlobalPosition, toGlobal, toLocal and getGlobalTransform walk up through the node's parents on each call, so their result is current even straight after a change. Reading worldTransform costs nothing and suits per-frame code that can use last frame's value.

visible hides a node and everything under it. Hiding and showing a node costs less than removing it and adding it back, so use visible for things that come and go often. Rendering throws while the view's camera or one of its parents is hidden, so keep the camera out of groups you hide. To take a node out for good, remove or destroy it. Resources and cleanup covers what that frees. The view's camera sits under view3d.root too, so clearing a level with view3d.root.removeChildren() takes the camera out, and the next render throws. Put each level in a Container3D of its own and clear that instead.

getLocalBounds measures a node and everything visible under it as a Box. It measures in the node's own space, before the node's own position, rotation and scale apply. Each call walks the subtree, so measure once rather than every frame. This scales a fox model to two units long and stands it on the ground at y = 0: import { Model3D } from '@pixi/3d'; const fox = new Model3D({ source }); const bounds = fox.getLocalBounds(); const scale = 2 / bounds.getSize().z; fox.scale.set(scale); fox.position.y = -bounds.min.y * scale; width, height and depth give the measured size times the scale. Setting one changes the scale on that axis only, and setSize sets all three. Both stretch a model unless the sizes you ask for keep its proportions. To keep them, work out one scale from the bounds, as above. Size and bounds fits three models into equal cubes, stretched with setSize or kept in shape with one scale.

Math: vectors, quaternions and turning a node with a quaternion. Cameras: placing and aiming the camera. View3D and 2D content: from world positions to the screen and back. Scene objects: the kinds of node a scene is built from.

A View3D is a PixiJS display object that draws a 3D scene. You add it to the stage, then move, scale, mask and filter it like a sprite. Everything in the scene goes under view3d.root. Calling view3d.addChild throws.

autoResize gives a view the renderer's screen size on every render, so a full-screen view follows the canvas when the window resizes. Without it, a view keeps the width and height you give it, 256 by 256 by default. anchor works as it does on a sprite. This keeps a centred view sized to the window, with a margin: import { View3D } from '@pixi/3d'; const view3d = new View3D({ anchor: 0.5 }); app.stage.addChild(view3d); const layout = (): void => { view3d.position.set(app.screen.width / 2, app.screen.height / 2); view3d.setSize(app.screen.width - 32, app.screen.height - 96); }; layout(); app.renderer.on('resize', layout); Three 2D habits work differently on a view: Setting width or height, or calling setSize, resizes the 3D viewport, the rectangle the camera draws into. It doesn't scale the view as it would a Sprite. It also turns autoResize off, so set autoResize back to true to follow the screen again. The scene doesn't stretch to the view's new shape. The camera sees more or less of it instead. Cameras explains which way, and how to keep a scene in frame. A rotated view still draws into the upright rectangle around it, so its background and any mesh reaching past its edges show in the corners outside the view. Mask the view to its own rectangle to hide them.

Each view is a separate scene, with its own root, camera, lights and environment, so a light in one view doesn't light another. A node belongs to one view at a time. Adding it under another view's root takes it out of the first, as addChild does in 2D. To show the same scene from a second angle, such as on a security monitor, don't build a second view. Give a second camera a renderTexture, add it under view3d.root and tell the view to draw from it. Second cameras shows how.

A view draws its whole scene at its place in the display list. 2D content added before the view draws behind the scene, and 2D content added after it draws over it: app.stage.addChild(backdrop); // behind the 3D scene app.stage.addChild(view3d); app.stage.addChild(scoreText); // over the 3D scene A view has no background by default, so the 2D content behind it shows wherever no mesh covers it. A mesh whose material has an alphaMode of 'blend' blends over that content. Glass, a material with transmission, can show that content through it. Physical extensions says when. Because a view draws its whole scene at once, no 2D object can go between two meshes of the same view. To put 2D content among 3D objects, draw it onto a 3D surface, as Rendering 2D into 3D shows. By default a view catches the pointer anywhere in its rectangle, even over empty space, so interactive 2D content behind it never gets the pointer. Interaction shows the ways around that.

PixiJS filters work on a view, or on a 2D container that holds one. Masks clip a view as they clip a sprite. This blurs a view: import { BlurFilter } from 'pixi.js'; view3d.filters = [new BlurFilter({ strength: 2, antialias: 'inherit', resolution: 'inherit' })]; Filters turns a blur, a black-and-white filter, a fade and a mask with rounded corners on and off on one view. By default a filter draws with one sample per pixel at a resolution of 1. On a canvas with a resolution above 1, a view under the filter loses its sharpness. It also loses the canvas's antialias smoothing unless the view is in composite mode. To keep both, create every filter on the view, or on a container holding it, with antialias: 'inherit' and resolution: 'inherit', as the blur above does. view3d.alpha and view3d.tint don't fade or tint a view. Give the view, or a container holding it, an AlphaFilter to fade it or a ColorMatrixFilter to tint it. For effects inside the 3D scene, such as bloom or ambient occlusion, add post effects. Post-processing covers them.

By default a view draws its scene at the resolution of its target, the thing it draws into, which is usually the canvas. Lower resolution when a device can't keep up. The scene then draws fewer pixels and stretches them over the view. The number is absolute, like a filter's resolution, so derive it from the renderer's: view3d.resolution = app.renderer.resolution * 0.67; // two thirds of the width and height A resolution other than the target's puts the view in composite mode. In composite mode the view draws its scene into a texture of its own, then draws that texture onto the target. composite: true and any enabled post effect do the same. This texture keeps the canvas's antialias. Post-processing says when it can't. 2D content behind the view still shows through, but not through glass. If the resolution changes while the app runs, create the view with composite: true. Without it, a view with no enabled post effect rebuilds its passes, the drawing steps of its frame, each time the resolution leaves or returns to the target's.

worldToScreen turns a point in the 3D world into PixiJS's global 2D coordinates, the space of event.global. It takes the view's anchor, position, scale and rotation into account. Use it to pin labels, health bars and markers to 3D objects, and add them after the view so they draw over it. A label added straight to an untouched app.stage can use the result as its position. Inside a moved, scaled or rotated container, convert the result with label.parent.toLocal(point, undefined, label.position). The point has to be in world space, the coordinates of the whole scene rather than of a node's parent. getGlobalPosition gives a node's world position. This code adds 0.6 to the y of a drone's world position to put its label just above the drone. The offset is in world units, so it doesn't turn or scale with the drone: import { Vector3 } from '@pixi/3d'; import { Point } from 'pixi.js'; const above = new Vector3(); const screen = new Point(); app.ticker.add(() => { drone.getGlobalPosition(above); above.y += 0.6; // just above the drone, in world units const point = view3d.worldToScreen(above, screen); label.visible = point !== null; if (point) label.position.copyFrom(point); }); app.ticker draws the frame after the code you add to it, so labels you place there match what it draws. That holds even when a camera controller moves the camera from Ticker.shared, which it does by default. If you pin labels to a view, size the view from the renderer's resize event, as Size and place a view does. With autoResize, a view takes the screen size only when it draws, so labels land in the wrong place on the first frame and lag a frame behind after each resize. To pin a label to a spot on a model, such as its head, convert that spot from the model's own space with toGlobal, which moves, turns and scales it with the model. Screen and world pins a name tag to the top of each clay piece this way. In perspective mode, the default, worldToScreen returns null for a point at or behind the camera. Hide the label when it does. A point off to one side of the camera's view still gets a position, outside the view's rectangle. Passing your own objects to write into, as the snippet does with above and screen, stops the per-frame code from allocating.

A point on the screen marks a ray, a line through the scene whose every point lands on that spot. screenToRay returns that Ray for a point in global coordinates, such as event.global. screenToWorld returns a point on the ray. Given a Plane, it returns where the ray meets the plane. Given a number instead, it returns the point that many units from the camera. Both methods work for a view that you move, scale or rotate on the stage. This moves a ring to the spot on the ground under the pointer: import { Plane, Vector3 } from '@pixi/3d'; const ground = new Plane(new Vector3(0, 1, 0), 0); // y = 0, facing up; a floor at y = h takes -h const hit = new Vector3(); view3d.on('pointermove', (event) => { const point = view3d.screenToWorld(event.global, ground, hit); ring.visible = point !== null && Math.hypot(point.x, point.z) < 5.6; // on a round floor of radius 5.6 if (point) ring.position.set(point.x, 0.04, point.z); }); With a plane, screenToWorld returns null when the ray misses the plane, such as when the pointer is above the horizon. The plane has no edges, so check that the point lies on your ground, as the radius check does for the round floor. With an OrbitCamera on the view, a drag that turns the camera can also end in a pointertap, and Interaction explains why. So Screen and world drops a shape on a pointertap only when the tap lands within a few pixels of its pointerdown. These methods never look at meshes. To find the object under the pointer, listen for pointer events on the objects, or call raycast. Interaction covers both.
Scene graph and transforms: positions, rotations and world space. Cameras: placing and aiming the camera. Rendering 2D into 3D: drawing PixiJS containers onto 3D surfaces.
PixiJS 3D draws with whichever GPU renderer PixiJS starts, WebGPU or WebGL2. Scenes, materials, lights and events use the same API on both.

Ask for WebGPU with PixiJS's preference option. PixiJS starts WebGPU where the browser has it and falls back to WebGL2 where it doesn't. If you leave preference out, PixiJS tries WebGL2 first, even in a browser that has WebGPU. On WebGPU, PixiJS 3D needs a GPU with the 'indirect-first-instance' feature. On a GPU without it, app.init throws instead of falling back to WebGL2. To fall back on those GPUs too, check for the feature before you start: import { Application, RendererType } from 'pixi.js'; const app = new Application(); const adapter = await navigator.gpu?.requestAdapter(); await app.init({ preference: adapter?.features.has('indirect-first-instance') ? 'webgpu' : 'webgl', resizeTo: window, }); const isWebGPU = app.renderer.type === RendererType.WEBGPU; app.renderer.type tells you which renderer started. To try a scene on WebGL2 in a browser that has WebGPU, start PixiJS with preference: 'webgl'. Installation covers how each renderer's code loads, and what to import when you start PixiJS with skipExtensionImports: true.

These are the differences you're most likely to meet: Your own shader code. A ShaderBit holds its code twice, gpu in WGSL for WebGPU and gl in GLSL for WebGL2. Write both. A bit that lacks one runs none of its code on that renderer, and you get no error. Toon and custom materials shows both. Glass. On WebGL2, glass refracts nothing in a view that draws straight onto an opaque canvas, which is what PixiJS does by default. Either PixiJS's useBackBuffer: true option or the view's composite: true fixes it. How glass draws covers both and says when to pick each. Float textures. Some features draw into floating-point textures. One is a cube map, six images of the surroundings, used as the view's environment. Another is any post effect whose stage is 'beforeToneMapping', the default for bloom and most other built-in effects. On WebGL2, PixiJS 3D draws into these textures only when the device has the EXT_color_buffer_float extension, and rendering throws on a device without it. Leave these features out on such a device. How a frame renders shows the check. Without the extension, a Hemisphere environment still lights the scene but loses its reflections, so a metal surface with no other light on it turns black. Polygon offset. A material's state.polygonOffset won't reliably keep a mark, such as a skid mark, in front of the surface it's drawn on. WebGPU ignores it. On WebGL2, a negative offset can push a mark behind a floor seen at an angle. Leave it at 0 and lift the mark's geometry a little off the surface instead. That works on both renderers.

Culling skips meshes outside the camera's frustum, the volume of space the camera sees, so the GPU never draws them. The view's cull mode is 'gpu' by default. In that mode, where the test runs depends on the renderer and the browser: WebGPU tests the meshes in a compute shader, a GPU program that calculates rather than draws. WebGPU in Safari, and in any browser on an iPhone or iPad, tests them on the CPU instead. That holds for a typical scene, and even for a BatchedMesh3D of ten thousand trees whose cull is 'gpu'. There, only a far larger batch culls in the compute shader. WebGL2 has no compute shaders, so it tests on the CPU in 'gpu' mode, the same as in 'cpu' mode. Blended meshes, whose material has an alphaMode of 'blend', are tested on the CPU on both renderers. When culling runs on the CPU, it tests every mesh every frame, even when nothing moves, so its cost grows with the number of meshes. CullMode says when to use each mode. Batching and culling sets Camera3D.cullFrustum to the frustum of a scout camera that sweeps round a field of clay pieces, so you can watch culling from outside that camera. Its pane switches cull between 'off', 'cpu' and 'gpu' and counts the pieces that survive.
Performance: draw calls, culling and a checklist for phones. How a frame renders: the passes a view runs each frame.
PixiJS 3D is the @pixi/3d package. It runs inside a PixiJS application, so you install it next to pixi.js.

npm install pixi.js @pixi/3d @pixi/3d needs pixi.js 8.23.0 or later. Import the engine from @pixi/3d, and the optional pieces from @pixi/3d/extras: import { Mesh3D, View3D } from '@pixi/3d'; import { OrbitCamera } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; import { Application } from 'pixi.js'; @pixi/3d/extras holds optional pieces built on the engine, such as the OrbitCamera and FPSCamera controllers, ParticleSystem3D, ToonMaterial, the BloomEffect and other post-processing effects, and debug tools such as GraphDebugOverlay.

PixiJS 3D has two backends, one for each of PixiJS's GPU renderers. One is the code that draws with WebGPU, and the other is the code that draws with WebGL2. Importing @pixi/3d registers neither. app.init loads and registers the backend for the renderer it starts. A production build from a bundler such as Vite puts each backend in a file of its own, as does the CDN build. A browser then downloads only the backend it uses. Import @pixi/3d before app.init runs. A renderer that started earlier never gets a backend, and a View3D on it draws nothing. This happens, for example, when the 3D code arrives in a lazily loaded chunk of a 2D app that's already running. skipExtensionImports: true stops PixiJS importing extensions for you, and stops app.init loading a backend, so you import the backends yourself. Each one you import goes in your main bundle. Import every backend the page can end up with. With preference: 'webgpu' that's both, since PixiJS falls back to WebGL2 where WebGPU is missing. Without the renderer's backend, a View3D draws nothing. import '@pixi/3d/webgl'; import '@pixi/3d/webgpu'; // PixiJS's events, filters, accessibility and DOM extensions are off too, so import the ones the page uses import 'pixi.js/events'; await app.init({ preference: 'webgpu', skipExtensionImports: true });

jsDelivr serves the CDN build from the dist folder of the npm package. Its files import pixi.js by name, so map pixi.js, @pixi/3d and @pixi/3d/extras in an import map. Then write the same code as with npm: <script type="importmap"> { "imports": { "pixi.js": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pixi.js@8.23.0/dist/pixi.min.mjs", "@pixi/3d": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@pixi/3d@0.1.0/dist/pixijs-3d.min.mjs", "@pixi/3d/extras": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@pixi/3d@0.1.0/dist/pixijs-3d-extras.min.mjs" } } </script> <script type="module"> import { View3D } from '@pixi/3d'; import { OrbitCamera } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; import { Application } from 'pixi.js'; // the same code as with npm </script> Import Application and the rest of PixiJS from the mapped pixi.js too. Loading PixiJS with a plain <script> tag defines a global PIXI, a second copy of PixiJS that PixiJS 3D doesn't register with. A View3D in an application made from it draws nothing. Map @pixi/3d and @pixi/3d/extras to files in the same folder, both minified or both unminified. The extras file imports the engine file next to it. If @pixi/3d maps to any other URL, such as one for another version, the page downloads and runs a second copy of the engine. To host the files yourself, keep every pixijs-3d file from dist together in one folder. The main file fetches the backend its renderer uses from its own folder, and the meshopt decoder for compressed models from there too. Draco-compressed models still fetch their decoder from Google until you host it too.

@pixi/3d ships its type declarations. They use the same WebGPU types as pixi.js, so a project set up the way the PixiJS TypeScript guide shows already has them. The types for @pixi/3d/extras come through the exports field of the package, so use a moduleResolution that reads them, such as "bundler". The older "node" setting can't find them.
Quick start: build a first scene. WebGL and WebGPU: what differs between the two backends.

PixiJS 3D, the @pixi/3d package, draws 3D scenes in a PixiJS application. A View3D holds the scene. It's a display object you add to the stage like a sprite. Hello cube shows the smallest scene, a cube and a light in a view.

2D content later in the display list draws over the scene. 2D content earlier in the list shows behind it, unless you give the view a background. By default the view catches pointer events anywhere in its rectangle, so the user can't click, tap or hover 2D content behind it. Interaction shows the ways around this. The scene inside a view is its own tree of Container3D nodes under the view's root. A 2D display object can't go in that tree, and a 3D node can't go on the stage. To show 2D content on a 3D surface, draw it into a ContainerTexture (Rendering 2D into 3D). To pin a 2D label over a 3D object, use worldToScreen (View3D and 2D content). Inside the scene, +Y points up, and the defaults expect one unit to be a metre, not a pixel. A camera draws nothing past its far distance, 1000 units by default, so it cuts off a scene built at pixel sizes.

Some parts come from @pixi/3d/extras, another entry point that Installation explains. Scene graph. Meshes, models, lights and cameras are all nodes. Each has a position, rotation and scale relative to its parent. See Scene graph and transforms and Scene objects. Meshes. A Mesh3D draws a geometry with a material. The geometry is the shape, and the material is how its surface looks. Built-in geometries such as CubeGeometry make common shapes, and a Geometry3D holds your own vertex data. See Meshes and Geometry. Resources and cleanup covers sharing geometries and materials between meshes and freeing their GPU memory. Sprites and batched meshes. A Sprite3D is a flat textured rectangle that turns to face the camera by default. BatchedMesh3D draws thousands of rigid meshes from one node. See Sprite3D and Batched meshes. Models. Assets.load reads glTF, an open standard format for 3D models, from .gltf and .glb files. A Model3D builds a loaded file's meshes, lights and cameras as nodes under itself. See Loading models and Compressed models. Animation. The model's player plays a file's animation clips by name and blends them. See Animation. Materials. Material3D is physically based, so it shades a surface the way real materials reflect light. PhongMaterial costs less per pixel, FlatMaterial draws with no lighting, and the extras add ToonMaterial for cartoon shading. See Materials. Lights and shadows. A DirectionalLight shines one way everywhere, like the sun. A PointLight shines every way from one point, like a bulb, and a SpotLight shines in a cone, like a torch. An AmbientLight shines from no direction. Directional and spot lights can cast shadows. See Lights and Shadows. Environment. The view's environment lights the scene from its surroundings. Use a Hemisphere for a sky-and-ground gradient, or a cube map for a picture of the surroundings on the six faces of a cube. See Environment. Cameras. A Camera3D's mode is perspective, where far things look smaller, or orthographic, where they don't. The extras' OrbitCamera lets the user drag the camera around a target point, and FPSCamera gives first-person controls. See Cameras and Camera controls. Interaction. 3D nodes take PixiJS's pointer events. Set a node's eventMode and listen on it as in 2D. See Interaction. Particles. The extras' ParticleSystem3D emits and moves particles for effects such as fire and snow, and ParticleContainer3D draws particles that your own code moves. See Particles. Post-processing. The extras hold effects and passes. An effect changes the finished picture, and BloomEffect is one that adds a glow. A pass is an extra drawing step that redraws meshes, and OutlinePass is one that draws ink outlines. Both go in the view's passes. See Post-processing. Math. PixiJS 3D has Vector3 and Matrix4, Quaternion for rotations, and shapes such as Ray, Plane and Box. See Math. Debugging. The extras' GraphDebugOverlay records frames and lists what each one drew. See Debugging. There's no physics engine; bring your own.
PixiJS 3D draws with WebGPU or WebGL2. WebGL and WebGPU covers choosing one. Performance explains what keeps a frame cheap and has a checklist for phones.

Installation: install @pixi/3d and the pixi.js version it needs. Quick start: build a first scene step by step, then load a model into it. View3D and 2D content: size a view and mix it with 2D content. Scene graph and transforms: the axes and units, and where 3D differs from 2D.

Most of a Three.js port is renaming. The hard part is code that still compiles and runs after the rename but draws a darker scene, a sideways light or a floor that casts a shadow. This page lists those differences first, then ports a small scene line by line. The API reference covers every name. The pixijs-3d agent skill that ships in the npm package also has full tables of Three.js names.

The scene is one display object in a PixiJS app. There's no renderer to own. Create an Application, add a View3D to its stage, and build the scene under view3d.root. 2D sprites, text and UI share the canvas, as View3D and 2D content explains. The view holds the scene-wide settings that Three.js splits between the renderer and the scene: toneMapping, exposure, shadowQuality, fog, background, environment and the post-processing passes. Constructors take one options object, such as new CubeGeometry({ width, height, depth }). The same values are properties on the object afterwards. The frame loop is app.ticker. Its callback gets the ticker. OrbitCamera, a model's player and ParticleSystem3D advance on Ticker.shared unless you step them yourself. A loaded glTF is a template. Assets.load returns a Scene3DSource, and each Model3D built from it shares its geometry, materials and textures. See Loading models.

Each line compiles after a plain rename and still changes what you see. The first group affects nearly every port. Light and shadow A HemisphereLight becomes the view's environment, a Hemisphere. Three.js divides its intensity by π and the view doesn't, so pass intensity: i / Math.PI. Directional, point, spot and ambient intensities port unchanged. Lights have no target. Directional and spot lights shine along their local -Z axis, so call lookAt after placing one, and again after every move (Lights). An unrotated DirectionalLight shines sideways, not down. Meshes and models cast and receive shadows by default. Set castShadow: false on floors and terrain, which otherwise also stretch the sun's shadow box. shadow.bias has the opposite sign, so negate a Three.js value or keep the default. shadow.mapSize becomes the view's shadowQuality, and the shadow camera's box becomes shadow.bounds, which is in world space. Time ticker.deltaTime measures time in 60 fps frames, not seconds. For the seconds that Three.js's getDelta() returns, use ticker.deltaMS / 1000. The ticker caps deltaMS at 100 ms, so below 10 fps motion slows down. Where Three.js called controls.update() or mixer.update(dt) in the loop, build the controller or model with autoUpdate: false. Then call its update(ticker) from app.ticker, so it steps in the same frame as your code. The camera defaults to a field of view of 60 and a far plane of 1000 (Camera3D.fov, Camera3D.far). Three.js apps usually pass 50 and 2000, so set both. Colour and output Tone mapping is off by default in both engines. exposure scales the light even under 'none', where Three.js ignores it, so port a NoToneMapping app with exposure 1. scene.background becomes the view's background, which post effects and fog cover as they do in Three.js. Under a tone mapping curve such as 'aces', the background goes through the curve too. For an exact colour, pass backgroundColor to app.init instead. An emissive colour is an opt-in group, emissive: { color, strength }, and its colour defaults to white. Pass the group only where the Three.js emissive isn't black. Surfaces alphaMode defaults to 'opaque', which ignores alpha and texture alpha. transparent: true becomes 'blend', and alphaTest becomes 'mask' with alphaCutoff. Images upload without Three.js's flipY, so a picture on a PlaneGeometry needs flipV: true (Textures on the built-in shapes). Mipmaps are off by default. Load a tiled or distant texture with Assets.load({ src, data: { autoGenerateMipmaps: true } }), or it shimmers. Texture repeat and offset become the material's uvTransform, a PixiJS Matrix that applies to all its textures. Base colour and emissive textures always decode as sRGB, so colorSpace has nothing to port to. Scene graph rotation and quaternion don't stay in sync. Nodes from a glTF file, and nodes you've called lookAt on, store their orientation in the quaternion, so rotation.y += a throws it away (Rotation and quaternion). getLocalBounds measures in the node's own space, without its own transform, where Box3.setFromObject measures in world space. A Three.js crossFadeTo becomes two playing states whose weights you ramp, and play() doesn't stop any other state (Blending and crossfades).

A Three.js scene with a hemisphere light, a shadowed sun, a ground, a spinning box and orbit controls: const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true }); renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2)); renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight); renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true; document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement); const scene = new THREE.Scene(); scene.background = new THREE.Color(0x9cc7ea); const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(50, window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight, 0.1, 100); camera.position.set(4, 3, 8); const controls = new OrbitControls(camera, renderer.domElement); scene.add(new THREE.HemisphereLight(0xdfeeff, 0x5a5040, 1.5)); const sun = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xfff4e0, 2.5); sun.position.set(4, 8, 5); sun.castShadow = true; scene.add(sun); const ground = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.PlaneGeometry(20, 20), new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x7a9a5a })); ground.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; ground.receiveShadow = true; scene.add(ground); const box = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1), new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xd9534f })); box.position.y = 0.5; box.castShadow = true; scene.add(box); window.addEventListener('resize', () => { camera.aspect = window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight; camera.updateProjectionMatrix(); renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight); }); const timer = new THREE.Timer(); renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => { timer.update(time); box.rotation.y += timer.getDelta(); controls.update(); renderer.render(scene, camera); }); Here's the same scene in PixiJS 3D. Comments mark each line that's more than a rename. import { CubeGeometry, DirectionalLight, Material3D, Mesh3D, PlaneGeometry, View3D } from '@pixi/3d'; import { OrbitCamera } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; import { Application } from 'pixi.js'; const app = new Application(); await app.init({ resizeTo: window, antialias: true, resolution: Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2), autoDensity: true, }); document.body.appendChild(app.canvas); const view3d = new View3D({ autoResize: true, // follows the app's size, so you need no resize listener background: 0x9cc7ea, environment: { skyColor: 0xdfeeff, groundColor: 0x5a5040, intensity: 1.5 / Math.PI }, // divide by π }); app.stage.addChild(view3d); view3d.camera.fov = 50; // the default is 60 view3d.camera.far = 100; view3d.camera.position.set(4, 3, 8); // before the controller, which keeps this offset const orbit = new OrbitCamera({ view: view3d, autoUpdate: false }); const sun = new DirectionalLight({ color: 0xfff4e0, intensity: 2.5, castShadow: true, position: { x: 4, y: 8, z: 5 } }); view3d.root.addChild(sun); sun.lookAt({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 }); // lights have no target, so aim it const ground = new Mesh3D({ geometry: new PlaneGeometry({ width: 20, height: 20 }), material: new Material3D({ baseColor: 0x7a9a5a }), rotation: { x: -Math.PI / 2, y: 0, z: 0 }, // lies in XY like Three.js's, so lay it flat castShadow: false, // meshes cast shadows by default }); view3d.root.addChild(ground); const box = new Mesh3D({ geometry: new CubeGeometry({ width: 1, height: 1, depth: 1 }), material: new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xd9534f }), position: { x: 0, y: 0.5, z: 0 }, }); view3d.root.addChild(box); app.ticker.add((ticker) => { box.rotation.y += ticker.deltaMS / 1000; // deltaTime counts frames orbit.update(ticker); // stepped here, like controls.update() });

Quick start: the same pieces built up one step at a time. Environment and IBL: tone mapping, exposure, fog and cube maps. Shadows: the shadow box, cascades and fixing artefacts. Materials: choosing between the physically based, Phong, flat and toon materials.
This page builds a cube spinning on a floor one step at a time, then loads a glTF model into the scene. Install pixi.js and @pixi/3d first, as Installation shows.

A 3D scene runs in an ordinary PixiJS application: import { Application } from 'pixi.js'; const app = new Application(); await app.init({ preference: 'webgpu', resizeTo: window, antialias: true, background: 0x1a1a2e, resolution: Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2), autoDensity: true, }); document.body.appendChild(app.canvas); preference: 'webgpu' picks WebGPU where the browser has it and WebGL2 elsewhere. PixiJS 3D draws with either. If the GPU lacks a WebGPU feature that PixiJS 3D needs, app.init throws instead of falling back. WebGL and WebGPU shows how to check first. Capping resolution at 2 means a 3x phone screen draws fewer than half its pixels.

A View3D is a display object that draws a 3D scene, so you add it to the stage like a sprite. Everything in the scene goes under its root. import { View3D } from '@pixi/3d'; const view3d = new View3D({ autoResize: true, shadowQuality: 'high', environment: { skyColor: 0xc9d6ff, groundColor: 0x3a2f45, intensity: 0.6 }, }); app.stage.addChild(view3d); autoResize gives the view the screen's size on every render, so it follows the canvas as resizeTo resizes it. View3D and 2D content covers sizing and placing views. environment is light from the surroundings. This one is a Hemisphere, which gives surfaces facing up the sky colour, surfaces facing down the ground colour, and the sides a mix of the two. Environment covers cube maps, which light the scene from an image of its surroundings. A shadowQuality of 'high' gives sharper shadows than the default and uses four times the memory.

Every view comes with a Camera3D, at view3d.camera. Move it up and back: view3d.camera.position.set(3, 3, 5); +Y is up, and a camera with no rotation looks along -Z, into the screen. The OrbitCamera added below turns it to face the cube. Without a controller, aim it with lookAt, as in view3d.camera.lookAt({ x: 0, y: 0.4, z: 0 }).

import { DirectionalLight } from '@pixi/3d'; const sun = new DirectionalLight({ color: 0xfff4e0, intensity: 3, castShadow: true }); sun.position.set(-3, 5, 2); view3d.root.addChild(sun); sun.lookAt({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 }); A DirectionalLight shines in one direction everywhere, like the sun. It points along its local -Z axis, and lookAt aims it. Its position changes neither its light nor where its shadow falls. Here it only gives lookAt a point to aim from. castShadow turns on the sun's shadow, and the sun fits that shadow around the meshes that cast one. The meshes below cast and receive shadows by default. Lights and Shadows cover the other lights and the shadow settings.

import { CubeGeometry, Material3D, Mesh3D, PlaneGeometry } from '@pixi/3d'; const floor = new Mesh3D({ geometry: new PlaneGeometry({ width: 8, height: 8 }), material: new Material3D({ baseColor: 0x888888, roughness: 0.85 }), castShadow: false, }); floor.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; view3d.root.addChild(floor); const cube = new Mesh3D({ geometry: new CubeGeometry({ width: 0.8, height: 0.8, depth: 0.8 }), material: new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xdd4444, roughness: 0.5 }), }); cube.position.y = 0.4; view3d.root.addChild(cube); A Mesh3D draws a geometry with a material. The geometry is its shape, and the material is how its surface looks. A Material3D's roughness runs from 0 for a mirror-like surface to 1 for a fully rough one. A PlaneGeometry is upright and faces +Z. Seen from behind, it draws nothing unless its material is doubleSided. Turning it -π/2 around X lays it flat, facing up. Turning it +π/2 instead faces it down, so the floor disappears when seen from above. The floor only receives shadows, so it turns castShadow off. The sun then fits its shadow to the cube instead of the whole floor, which keeps the shadow sharp. A CubeGeometry is centred on its origin, so lifting the cube by half its height sets it on the floor.
documents.s: Add a floor and a cube

documents.t: Animate from the application's ticker, as in 2D: app.ticker.add((ticker) => { cube.rotation.y += 0.5 * (ticker.deltaMS / 1000); });

import { OrbitCamera } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; new OrbitCamera({ view: view3d, target: { x: 0, y: 0.4, z: 0 }, enableDamping: true, minDistance: 2, maxDistance: 15, }); OrbitCamera, from @pixi/3d/extras, moves the view's camera around a target point. Drag to orbit, and scroll or pinch to zoom. It starts from where the camera is and always turns it to face the target. enableDamping keeps the camera turning for a moment after the pointer stops and slows it to a stop. minDistance and maxDistance keep it between 2 and 15 units from the target. PixiJS listens for wheel events but doesn't block them, so a page that can scroll also scrolls as you zoom. For a full-window canvas, stop the page from scrolling, for example with body { margin: 0; overflow: hidden; }. In Chrome, a trackpad pinch also zooms the whole page. Orbit camera shows a canvas listener that stops the page from scrolling and zooming. Camera controls covers panning, the other settings and a first-person controller.

import { Model3D } from '@pixi/3d'; import type { Scene3DSource } from '@pixi/3d'; import { Assets } from 'pixi.js'; // Fox by PixelMannen (CC0), rigging and animation by tomkranis (CC BY 4.0), glTF conversion by // @AsoboStudio and @scurest (CC BY 4.0) const source = await Assets.load<Scene3DSource>( 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/KhronosGroup/glTF-Sample-Assets@edc7c9e67c639d230715049ee31f9a96a6babbbe/Models/Fox/glTF-Binary/Fox.glb', ); const fox = new Model3D({ source }); fox.scale.set(0.8 / fox.height); fox.position.x = 1.5; view3d.root.addChild(fox); fox.player?.play('Walk'); glTF is an open file format for 3D models, saved as .gltf or a single binary .glb. Importing @pixi/3d registers loaders for both with Assets. Assets.load returns a Scene3DSource that holds the file's data. A Model3D is a container that builds the file's meshes, lights and cameras inside itself. A model keeps the units it was made in, and the fox's height is about 80. To get the scale, divide the height you want, here the cube's 0.8, by the model's height. When the file has animations, the model's player plays them by name. Animation shows how to list the names and blend clips. To show one model on its own, View3D.from builds a view around it with a camera and a light. Loading models covers both ways.

Scene graph and transforms: grouping nodes, the axes, and the two ways to rotate. Materials: choosing a material and its features. Loading models: sources, models, compressed files and cleaning up. Interaction: clicking, hovering and dragging 3D objects. Performance: keeping a scene fast on phones, and which node to use for many objects.
Build 3D scenes one step at a time, from your first lit shape to a playable game. Every step comes with a live editor and a solution.
Build a scene of soft clay shapes floating behind 2D text, with a view, lights, materials, primitive geometry and a camera that follows the pointer. 8 steps · 20 minStart
Show an animated glTF model on a stand, lit by a photo of a real place, with an orbiting camera, 2D buttons that crossfade its animations, and a label that follows it. 8 steps · 30 minStart

Build a fairground shooting gallery: a lit booth, targets that slide along two rails and fall when you hit them, confetti, a score in 2D and on a 3D board, bloom, and a timed round. 8 steps · 40 minStart

Welcome to Floating Shapes. You'll build a scene of soft clay shapes drifting around a 2D headline, with a camera that leans toward your pointer. Your code runs inside an async function that runs as soon as it's defined, an IIFE, so it can await the setup.

PixiJS 3D draws inside an ordinary PixiJS application. The starting code creates one; initialize it next: await app.init({ preference: 'webgpu', resizeTo: window, antialias: true, background: 0xf3edff, resolution: Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2), autoDensity: true, }); preference: 'webgpu' asks for WebGPU. In a browser without it, PixiJS uses WebGL2, and PixiJS 3D draws with either. resolution draws at the screen's pixel density, capped at 2 to limit how many pixels a phone with a very dense screen has to draw. Then add the canvas to the page: document.body.appendChild(app.canvas); The preview fills with pale lavender. In the next step you'll put a 3D view on top of it.

Welcome to Model Showroom. You'll load an animated fox from a glTF file, the usual file format for 3D models, and light it with a photo of a real place. Then you'll put it on a stand and add a camera that circles it, 2D buttons that switch its animations, and a label pinned to its head. This tutorial assumes you've built a scene with a View3D before; Floating Shapes covers the basics. The starting code creates the application. Work in index.ts, below it.

Before the fox arrives, two balls will show what the light in the scene looks like. Add a view, the balls and a sun: const view3d = new View3D({ autoResize: true }); app.stage.addChild(view3d); view3d.camera.position.set(0, 0, 5); const geometry = new SphereGeometry({ radius: 0.55 }); const mirror = new Mesh3D({ geometry, material: new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xffffff, metallic: 1, roughness: 0.05 }), }); const matte = new Mesh3D({ geometry, material: new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xf06695, roughness: 0.6 }) }); mirror.x = -0.65; matte.x = 0.65; view3d.root.addChild(mirror, matte); const sun = new DirectionalLight({ intensity: 2 }); sun.position.set(1, 1, 0.4); view3d.root.addChild(sun); sun.lookAt({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 }); The two balls share one SphereGeometry, the way two sprites share a texture, and each has its own Material3D. metallic at 1 makes a metal, and a roughness near 0 polishes it. A metal shows only what it reflects, and a polished one reflects like a mirror. The matte ball is a non-metal, the default, and its rougher surface spreads out the light it reflects. The DirectionalLight shines from the upper right toward the middle of the scene. The pink ball is lit on its upper right. The mirror ball is black apart from one small bright dot, its reflection of the sun, because there's nothing else around it to reflect. In the next step you'll give it something.
documents.s: A view and two test balls

documents.t: You'll build a fairground booth at night, with targets sliding along two rails. Hit a target and it falls back in a burst of confetti, the score goes up on a board over the booth, and the round ends after 30 seconds. This tutorial assumes you've built a scene with a View3D before; Floating Shapes covers the basics. The starting code sets up the stage: index.ts creates the application and a view with a crosshair cursor. A Hemisphere environment lights the scene like a dim night sky: surfaces facing up take its sky colour, and surfaces facing down its ground colour. camera.ts places the camera in front of the booth, and moves it back on narrow screens so the whole booth fits. In this step you'll build the booth itself in buildBooth, in booth.ts.

Start with the materials the booth is made of: const wood = new Material3D({ baseColor: 0x9a5b34, roughness: 0.7 }); const cream = new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xf2e6cf, roughness: 0.5 }); const red = new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xd81b3c, roughness: 0.45, clearcoat: { factor: 0.6, roughness: 0.2 } }); const wall = new Material3D({ baseColor: 0x3a2c6e, roughness: 0.9 }); const brass = new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xe0b060, metallic: 1, roughness: 0.35 }); const bulb = new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xffffff, emissive: { color: 0xffc46b, strength: 2 } }); Material3D is the lit material you met in Floating Shapes. metallic: 1 makes the brass a metal, and the red paint has a glossy clear coat. emissive adds the material's own glow on top of the lighting, so the bulbs show even where no light reaches them. It doesn't light anything around them. The bulb colour's red channel is already full, so a strength above 1 pushes the glow past white, which matters when you add bloom in the "Add juice" step.

Meshes can share a geometry. A CubeGeometry is 1 unit on each side by default, so one cube, scaled to size, makes every box in the booth. One CylinderGeometry makes both posts. The booth stands on y = 0, and the camera looks along -z, so x runs across the booth, y up it and z toward you. A small helper makes a mesh, places it and adds it to the scene: const cube = new CubeGeometry(); const post = new CylinderGeometry({ radiusTop: 0.14, radiusBottom: 0.14, height: 5.2, radialSegments: 24 }); const add = (geometry, material, x, y, z) => { const mesh = new Mesh3D({ geometry, material }); mesh.position.set(x, y, z); view3d.root.addChild(mesh); return mesh; }; add(cube, wall, 0, 2.5, -1.3).scale.set(9, 5, 0.2); add(cube, wall, -4.3, 2.5, 0.1).scale.set(0.2, 5, 2.8); add(cube, wall, 4.3, 2.5, 0.1).scale.set(0.2, 5, 2.8); add(cube, red, 0, 0.6, 1.5).scale.set(8.8, 1.2, 0.7); add(cube, wood, 0, 1.26, 1.45).scale.set(9.2, 0.12, 1); add(post, cream, -4.5, 2.6, 1.6); add(post, cream, 4.5, 2.6, 1.6); add(cube, brass, 0, 1.6, -0.7).scale.set(8.6, 0.08, 0.08); add(cube, brass, 0, 3.05, -0.7).scale.set(8.6, 0.08, 0.08); The last two boxes are thin brass rails for the targets to run along.

A row of stripes in alternating colours, tipped forward at the bottom, with bulbs along its edge: for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) { const stripe = add(cube, i % 2 ? cream : red, (i - 3.5) * 1.15, 5.45, 1.75); stripe.scale.set(1.15, 0.9, 0.06); stripe.rotation.x = -0.4; } const bulbGeometry = new SphereGeometry({ radius: 0.07, widthSegments: 12, heightSegments: 8 }); for (let i = 0; i < 9; i++) add(bulbGeometry, bulb, (i - 4) * 1.15, 5.03, 1.95); Rotations are in radians, as in 2D. A negative rotation around x tips the top of a stripe away from you.

A SpotLight shines in a cone from a point, like a stage light. Put one high up on each side, in front of the booth, aimed across it to where the targets will run: for (const side of [-1, 1]) { const spot = new SpotLight({ color: 0xffe2b8, intensity: 50, range: 18, coneAngle: 32, penumbra: 0.5, castShadow: true, }); spot.position.set(side * 3.6, 4.8, 7); spot.lookAt({ x: -side * 0.6, y: 2.4, z: -1.2 }); view3d.root.addChild(spot); } A spotlight shines along its own -z axis, so lookAt aims it at a point. Its light dims with the square of the distance, so a light about 9 units from the targets needs a much higher intensity than a directional light. It fades to nothing at its range. coneAngle is the angle from the middle of the cone to its edge, in degrees, and penumbra softens the edge. With castShadow, each spotlight casts its own shadow. A mesh made with new Mesh3D casts shadows by default, so each target you add next throws two. The preview shows a red and cream booth, lit warm from both sides against the night.

Canvas elements are invisible to screen readers by default. PixiJS bridges this gap with a DOM-based overlay system: it places invisible <div> elements over your canvas, aligned to the bounds of accessible objects. These divs integrate with screen readers, keyboard navigation (Tab key), and other assistive technologies so that users who can't see the canvas can still interact with your application. These overlay elements: Receive focus via keyboard (tabIndex) Announce accessibleTitle or accessibleHint to screen readers Dispatch click, mouseover, mouseout events as PixiJS pointer events Use aria-live and aria-label where appropriate important The AccessibilitySystem is not available in a Web Worker. It requires the main thread where the DOM is accessible.

Accessibility is an opt-in module to keep the default bundle small. Import it before creating your renderer: import 'pixi.js/accessibility'; PixiJS automatically installs the AccessibilitySystem onto your renderer.

Enable accessibility on any container or display object: import { Container } from 'pixi.js'; const button = new Container(); button.accessible = true; button.accessibleTitle = 'Play Game'; button.accessibleHint = 'Press to start the game'; button.accessibleType = 'button'; app.stage.addChild(button);

Property Default Description accessible false Enables accessibility for the object. accessibleTitle null Sets the title attribute for screen readers. accessibleHint null Sets the aria-label attribute. accessibleText null Alternative inner text for the div. accessibleType 'button' Tag name for the shadow element ('button', 'div', etc.). accessiblePointerEvents 'auto' CSS pointer-events value ('auto', 'none', etc.). tabIndex 0 Keyboard focus order. accessibleChildren true Whether children of this container are accessible.

Configure the accessibility system when creating your application: const app = new Application(); await app.init({ accessibilityOptions: { enabledByDefault: true, // Enable on startup instead of waiting for tab activateOnTab: true, // Allow tab key to activate accessibility debug: false, // Show accessibility divs for debugging deactivateOnMouseMove: true, // Disable when mouse is used }, });
Control the tab order of accessible elements: menuButton.tabIndex = 1; playButton.tabIndex = 2; settingsButton.tabIndex = 3;

Control accessibility for nested elements: const menu = new Container(); menu.accessible = true; menu.accessibleChildren = true; // Allow children to be accessible (default) // Setting to false prevents all children from being accessible menu.accessibleChildren = false;

Enable or disable the system at runtime: app.renderer.accessibility.setAccessibilityEnabled(true); console.log(app.renderer.accessibility.isActive); console.log(app.renderer.accessibility.isMobileAccessibility);
Use debug mode during development to see the overlay divs: await app.init({ accessibilityOptions: { debug: true, }, });
AccessibilitySystem AccessibleOptions AccessibilityOptions

The Application class is the starting point for most PixiJS projects. It sets up a renderer, creates a scene graph, and runs a frame loop so you can focus on building your game or visualization. It supports WebGL, WebGPU, and Canvas2D through async initialization.

Creating an application requires two steps: constructing an instance, then initializing it with .init(): import { Application } from 'pixi.js'; const app = new Application(); await app.init({ width: 800, height: 600, backgroundColor: 0x1099bb, }); document.body.appendChild(app.canvas);
The application provides a root container (stage) where you add all your visual elements: import { Sprite } from 'pixi.js'; const sprite = Sprite.from('image.png'); app.stage.addChild(sprite);

By default, the TickerPlugin handles the rendering loop: import { Application, Ticker } from 'pixi.js'; await app.init({ autoStart: true, sharedTicker: false, }); // Start/stop the rendering loop app.start(); app.stop(); // Access ticker properties console.log(app.ticker.FPS); console.log(app.ticker.deltaMS); // Add update callbacks app.ticker.add(() => { // Animation logic here }); app.ticker.addOnce(() => { // Runs once after the next frame });

The ResizePlugin enables automatic resizing to fit different containers or the window: // Auto-resize to window await app.init({ resizeTo: window }); // Auto-resize to a container element await app.init({ resizeTo: document.querySelector('#game') }); // Manual resize control app.resize(); app.queueResize(); app.cancelResize();

The .init() method accepts a Partial<ApplicationOptions> object: Option Type Default Description autoStart boolean true Start rendering after initialization. Setting to false won't stop the shared ticker if it's running. resizeTo Window | HTMLElement - Element to auto-resize the renderer to match. sharedTicker boolean false Use the shared ticker instance if true; otherwise a private ticker is created. preference RendererPreference | RendererPreference[] webgl Preferred renderer type(s). Pass an array to restrict to specific renderers. useBackBuffer boolean false (WebGL only) Use the back buffer when required. forceFallbackAdapter boolean false (WebGPU only) Force usage of fallback adapter. canvasOptions Partial<CanvasOptions> - Options passed only to the Canvas renderer. powerPreference 'high-performance' | 'low-power' undefined Hint for GPU power preference (WebGL and WebGPU). antialias boolean - Enable anti-aliasing. May impact performance. autoDensity boolean - Adjust canvas size based on resolution. Applies only to HTMLCanvasElement. background ColorSource - Alias for backgroundColor. backgroundAlpha number 1 Alpha transparency for background (0 = transparent, 1 = opaque). backgroundColor ColorSource 'black' Color used to clear the canvas. Accepts hex, CSS color, or array. canvas ICanvas - A custom canvas instance. clearBeforeRender boolean true Clear the canvas each frame before rendering. context WebGL2RenderingContext | null null User-supplied rendering context (WebGL). depth boolean - Enable a depth buffer in the main view. Always true for WebGL. transient boolean false (WebGPU only, with antialias) Discard the canvas's multisample depth/stencil buffer at the end of each pass, and its colour buffer on GPUs that aren't tile-based (tile-based GPUs already discard colour). Only for apps that never reopen the canvas pass while still needing depth or stencil: no filters or masks popping back onto it, no render with clear: false. format TEXTURE_FORMATS - (WebGPU only) Canvas format: bgra8unorm, rgba8unorm or rgba16float. Defaults to the browser's preferred format, as the other 8-bit format can cost an extra full-screen copy every frame. Use rgba16float for an HDR canvas. height number 600 Height of the renderer in pixels. width number 800 Width of the renderer in pixels. hello boolean false Log renderer info and version to the console. multiView boolean false Enable multi-canvas rendering. premultipliedAlpha boolean true Assume alpha is premultiplied in color buffers. preserveDrawingBuffer boolean false Preserve buffer between frames. Needed for toDataURL. resolution number 1 Pixel ratio for rendering. Set to window.devicePixelRatio for crisp output on high-DPI screens. Use with autoDensity: true. skipExtensionImports boolean false Prevent automatic import of default PixiJS extensions. Renderer loader extensions (WebGLLoader, WebGPULoader, CanvasLoader) are skipped too. textureGCActive boolean true (Deprecated) Enable garbage collection for GPU textures. Use gcActive. textureGCCheckCountMax number 600 (Deprecated) Frame interval between GC runs. Use gcFrequency. textureGCMaxIdle number 3600 (Deprecated) Max idle frames before destroying a texture. Use gcMaxUnusedTime. webgl Partial<WebGLOptions> - Override options applied only when using the WebGL renderer. webgpu Partial<WebGPUOptions> - Override options applied only when using the WebGPU renderer.

You can override properties per renderer using the webgl, webgpu, or canvasOptions keys: const app = new Application(); await app.init({ width: 800, height: 600, backgroundColor: 0x1099bb, webgl: { antialias: true, }, webgpu: { antialias: false, }, canvasOptions: { // Canvas2D-specific options }, }); document.body.appendChild(app.canvas);

Set preference to 'canvas' to use the HTML Canvas 2D context instead of WebGL or WebGPU: const app = new Application(); await app.init({ width: 800, height: 600, preference: 'canvas', }); The Canvas renderer is a fallback for environments where neither WebGL nor WebGPU is available. If you don't set a preference, PixiJS tries WebGL first, then WebGPU, then Canvas. note The Canvas renderer supports a subset of PixiJS features. Filters, advanced blend modes, and some shader-based effects are unavailable.

When you're done with the application, clean up resources: // Basic cleanup app.destroy(); // Full cleanup with options app.destroy( { removeView: true }, // removes the canvas element from the DOM { children: true, // destroy all children in the stage texture: true, // destroy textures used by children textureSource: true, // destroy the underlying GPU texture sources }, );
PixiJS includes these plugins: Ticker Plugin - Updates every frame. Guide Resize Plugin - Resizes renderer/canvas. Guide Culler Plugin (optional) - Culls offscreen objects. Guide

Custom plugins for Application must be classes with static init() and destroy() methods, plus a static extension property set to ExtensionType.Application. Both methods are called with this set to the Application instance, so this.renderer and this.stage are available. import { ExtensionType, extensions } from 'pixi.js'; import type { ApplicationOptions } from 'pixi.js'; class MyPlugin { public static extension = ExtensionType.Application; public static init(options: Partial<ApplicationOptions>) { console.log('Custom plugin init:', this, options); } public static destroy() { console.log('Custom plugin destroy'); } } extensions.add(MyPlugin);

If you're using TypeScript or providing a plugin for others, extend the ApplicationOptions interface to include your plugin's options: declare global { namespace PixiMixins { interface ApplicationOptions { myPlugin?: import('./myPlugin').PluginOptions | null; } } } await app.init({ myPlugin: { customOption: true, }, });
Application ApplicationOptions AutoDetectOptions WebGLOptions WebGPUOptions CanvasOptions SharedRendererOptions TickerPlugin ResizePlugin CullerPlugin

The CullerPlugin improves performance by skipping offscreen objects during rendering. It checks whether each container (and its children) intersects the visible screen area. Objects outside the view are marked as hidden ("culled"), so the renderer skips them entirely. This reduces draw calls and update overhead. PixiJS does not enable this plugin by default. You must register it manually with the extensions system.
Culling works well for: Large scenes with many offscreen elements Scrollable or camera-driven environments (e.g. tilemaps, world views) Reducing render cost without restructuring your scene graph

import { Application, Container, Sprite, extensions, CullerPlugin } from 'pixi.js'; extensions.add(CullerPlugin); const app = new Application(); await app.init({ width: 800, height: 600, backgroundColor: 0x222222, }); const world = new Container(); world.cullable = true; const sprite = Sprite.from('path/to/image.png'); sprite.cullable = true; world.addChild(sprite); app.stage.addChild(world);

import { extensions, CullerPlugin } from 'pixi.js'; extensions.add(CullerPlugin); This overrides the render() method on your Application instance to call Culler.shared.cull() before rendering: // Internally replaces: app.renderer.render({ container: app.stage }); // With: Culler.shared.cull(app.stage, app.renderer.screen); app.renderer.render({ container: app.stage });

By default, containers are not culled (cullable is false). cullableChildren defaults to true, so you only need to set cullable on the containers you want culled: container.cullable = true; // This container will be culled when offscreen To disable recursive child culling: container.cullableChildren = false; // Children won't be individually culled

You can define a cullArea to override the default bounds check (which uses global bounds): import { Rectangle } from 'pixi.js'; container.cullArea = new Rectangle(0, 0, 100, 100); This helps when bounding box calculations for a container's children are expensive or inaccurate.

If you're not using the plugin but want to cull before rendering manually: import { Culler } from 'pixi.js'; const stage = new Container(); // Configure stage and children... Culler.shared.cull(stage, { x: 0, y: 0, width: 800, height: 600 }); renderer.render({ container: stage });
CullerPlugin Culler

The ResizePlugin auto-resizes PixiJS applications. It listens to window or element resize events and adjusts the renderer to match. Useful for: Making the canvas responsive to the browser window Fitting to container elements Handling layout changes without manual resize calls PixiJS includes this plugin by default when initializing an Application. You can also register it manually for custom setups.
import { Application } from 'pixi.js'; const app = new Application(); await app.init({ width: 800, height: 600, resizeTo: window, });

The ResizePlugin is installed automatically with Application.init(). When resizeTo is set, the renderer adjusts to match the target (window or HTMLElement). Resizing is throttled with requestAnimationFrame to avoid performance issues during rapid resize events. You can trigger a resize manually with app.resize() or cancel a scheduled resize with app.cancelResize().
If you're managing extensions manually: import { extensions, ResizePlugin } from 'pixi.js'; extensions.add(ResizePlugin);
Resize the canvas to fit a specific element instead of the window: await app.init({ resizeTo: document.getElementById('game-container'), });

You can reassign resizeTo after initialization: app.resizeTo = window; // resize to window app.resizeTo = document.getElementById('game-container'); // resize to an element app.resizeTo = null; // disable auto-resize Setting resizeTo removes the previous listener and attaches a new one to the given target. Setting it to null removes the listener entirely; the canvas stays at its current size until you resize it manually with app.resize() or set a new resizeTo target.
documents.s: Changing the resize target at runtime

documents.t: The plugin throttles resize events so only one resize fires per animation frame: app.queueResize(); // schedule a resize for the next frame app.cancelResize(); // cancel a pending resize This is handled automatically when the window or element emits a resize event. You only need to call these methods when triggering resizes from your own code.

When the resizeTo target is window, the plugin reads innerWidth and innerHeight. For an HTMLElement, it reads clientWidth and clientHeight. The renderer is resized to those dimensions, then a render pass runs to reflect the new size.
ResizePlugin ResizePluginOptions

The TickerPlugin provides a built-in update loop for your PixiJS Application. It calls .render() once per animation frame by default and integrates with PixiJS's Ticker system for frame-based control. PixiJS includes this plugin automatically when you initialize an Application. You can also opt out and add it manually.
const app = new Application(); await app.init({ sharedTicker: false, autoStart: true, }); app.ticker.add((ticker) => { bunny.rotation += 1 * ticker.deltaTime; });
The TickerPlugin is included automatically: const app = new Application(); await app.init({ autoStart: true, // Starts the render loop automatically sharedTicker: false, // Use a dedicated ticker });
If you're managing extensions yourself: import { extensions, TickerPlugin } from 'pixi.js'; extensions.add(TickerPlugin);

The plugin supports two modes: Option Description sharedTicker: true Uses Ticker.shared, shared across all applications. sharedTicker: false Creates a private ticker instance scoped to the application.
With a shared ticker, other code can also register updates, so execution order can vary. With a dedicated ticker, you get full control over timing and update order.

When using a shared ticker, updates run in this order: System ticker (Ticker.system) -- internal PixiJS updates like interaction events and accessibility. Always runs first. Shared ticker (Ticker.shared) -- your callbacks if sharedTicker: true. App ticker -- a private Ticker instance created per-app if sharedTicker: false.
Stop and start the ticker manually: app.stop(); // Stop automatic rendering app.start(); // Resume Useful for: Pausing a game or animation Throttling on inactive tabs Managing visibility events

If you disable autoStart, you can manage the render loop yourself: const app = new Application(); await app.init({ autoStart: false }); function animate() { app.ticker.update(); // fire any registered ticker callbacks app.render(); requestAnimationFrame(animate); } animate();

Register callbacks to run every frame: // Runs every frame app.ticker.add((ticker) => { sprite.x += speed * ticker.deltaTime; }); // Runs once on the next frame, then auto-removes app.ticker.addOnce(() => { console.log('Ready'); });

Control the order callbacks run in using UPDATE_PRIORITY: import { UPDATE_PRIORITY } from 'pixi.js'; app.ticker.add( (ticker) => { // Physics: runs before normal-priority updates }, null, UPDATE_PRIORITY.HIGH );
TickerPlugin TickerPluginOptions Ticker UPDATE_PRIORITY

The Assets singleton is how you load images, spritesheets, fonts, and other resources in PixiJS. It's Promise-based, caches results automatically, and picks the best file format for the user's device. Most PixiJS projects use Assets.load() as their first step after creating an Application. import { Assets, Texture } from 'pixi.js'; await Assets.init({ basePath: 'assets/', }); // Load a single asset const texture = await Assets.load<Texture>('bunny.png'); // Load multiple assets const assets = await Assets.load(['bunny.png', 'spritesheet.json', 'font.ttf']);

Type Extensions Loaders Textures .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .avif, .svg loadTextures, loadSvg Video Textures .mp4, .m4v, .webm, .ogg, .ogv, .h264, .avi, .mov loadVideoTextures Sprite Sheets .json spritesheetAsset Bitmap Fonts .fnt, .xml loadBitmapFont Web Fonts .ttf, .otf, .woff, .woff2 loadWebFont JSON .json loadJson Text .txt loadTxt Compressed Textures .basis, .dds, .ktx, .ktx2 loadBasis, loadDDS, loadKTX, loadKTX2 You can add custom parsers for additional formats via LoaderParser.

Call Assets.load() with a URL or array of URLs. It returns a Promise that resolves to the loaded resource. import { Application, Assets, Sprite, Texture } from 'pixi.js'; const app = new Application(); await app.init({ backgroundColor: 0x1099bb }); // Load a single asset const bunnyTexture = await Assets.load<Texture>('path/to/bunny.png'); const sprite = new Sprite(bunnyTexture); // Load multiple assets at once const textures = await Assets.load<Texture>(['path/to/bunny.png', 'path/to/cat.png']); const bunnySprite = new Sprite(textures['path/to/bunny.png']); const catSprite = new Sprite(textures['path/to/cat.png']); PixiJS determines how to load the asset based on its file extension and caches the result to avoid redundant downloads.

Assets caches by URL or alias. Requests for the same resource return the same instance: const p1 = await Assets.load('bunny.png'); const p2 = await Assets.load('bunny.png'); console.log(p1 === p2); // true

Use aliases to reference assets by name instead of full URLs: await Assets.load<Texture>({ alias: 'bunny', src: 'path/to/bunny.png' }); const bunnyTexture = Assets.get('bunny'); All Asset APIs support aliases, including Assets.load(), Assets.get(), and Assets.unload(). For more complex resolution rules, see the Resolver guide.
Retrieve previously loaded assets with Assets.get(): await Assets.load<Texture>('path/to/bunny.png'); const bunnyTexture = Assets.get('path/to/bunny.png'); const sprite = new Sprite(bunnyTexture);
Assets.unload() removes an asset from the cache and frees memory: await Assets.unload('path/to/bunny.png');

Asset loading can fail for many reasons (network issues, corrupt files, unsupported formats). The loader provides configurable behavior through LoadOptions. Supply these per call or globally via Assets.init or Loader.defaultOptions. Supported options: onProgress(progress: number): Called as each asset completes (0.0 to 1.0) onError(error: Error, asset): Called when an individual asset fails strategy: 'throw' | 'skip' | 'retry' retryCount: Number of retry attempts when strategy is 'retry' (default 3) retryDelay: Delay in ms between retries (default 250)

Strategy Behavior Error propagation Use when throw First failure rejects the load promise Yes (immediate) Critical assets must all succeed skip Failed assets are ignored; others continue No (but onError fires) Optional / best-effort assets retry Retries each failing asset up to retryCount, then throws if still failing Yes (after final attempt) Transient network/CDN instability await Assets.init({ loadOptions: { strategy: 'retry', retryCount: 4, retryDelay: 400, onError: (err, asset) => console.debug('Retrying:', asset.src), }, }); // Later calls inherit these unless overridden await Assets.load('critical.json'); // Skip missing optional texture const tex = await Assets.load('optional.png', { strategy: 'skip', onError: (err, asset) => console.warn('Skipped:', asset, err.message), });

Group related assets into bundles for organized loading: Assets.addBundle('loading-screen', [ { alias: 'background', src: 'bg.png' }, { alias: 'progress-bar', src: 'bar.png' }, ]); Assets.addBundle('game', [ { alias: 'character', src: 'hero.png' }, { alias: 'enemies', src: 'monsters.json' }, ]); const loadingAssets = await Assets.loadBundle('loading-screen'); const gameAssets = await Assets.loadBundle('game'); For manifest-based bundles, see the Manifests & Bundles guide.

Load assets in the background while the application runs: Assets.backgroundLoad(['level1.json', 'level2.json']); // Later, these resolve immediately if already loaded const level1 = await Assets.load('level1.json'); const level2 = await Assets.load('level2.json'); See the Background Loading guide for details.

Provide options to Assets.init() to configure the loading process: import { Assets } from 'pixi.js'; await Assets.init({ basePath: 'assets/', texturePreference: { format: ['webp', 'png'], resolution: 2, }, defaultSearchParams: { version: '1.0.0', }, }); Option Type Description basePath string Prefix applied to all relative asset paths (e.g. for CDNs) defaultSearchParams string | Record<string, any> Default URL parameters to append to all asset requests skipDetections boolean Skip environment detection parsers for assets manifest AssetsManifest A descriptor of named asset bundles and their contents preferences AssetsPreferences Format and resolution preferences for loading bundleIdentifier BundleIdentifierOptions Override how bundle IDs are generated loadOptions LoadOptions Default load strategy, retry behavior, and error handling

// Check if asset is cached const isCached = Assets.cache.has('texture.png'); // Get cached asset const texture = Assets.get('texture.png'); // Unload specific assets await Assets.unload('texture.png'); // Reset entire cache Assets.reset();

Call Assets.init() before loading any assets Use bundles for organized loading Use format fallbacks (e.g., image.{webp,png}) Use background loading for non-critical assets Clean up unused assets with Assets.unload() Use manifests for larger applications
Assets AssetsManifest LoaderParser CacheParser BackgroundLoader Texture Spritesheet loadTextures loadWebFont

The background loader queues asset downloads at low priority so they happen between frames while your application runs. Assets added to the background queue are not downloaded immediately – they are fetched one at a time (or up to the configured concurrency limit) while the main application continues. Only once each item has actually finished downloading is it placed into the regular cache. Important: a background‑queued asset is not instantly available just because you called Assets.backgroundLoad. If you call Assets.load() or Assets.loadBundle() for the same asset before the background fetch has completed, the loader will treat it as a high‑priority request and perform a fresh download (pausing the background process); the call only resolves instantly when the background load has already finished.

The most effective way to use the background loader is with bundles. Bundles are groups of related assets, such as all assets for a specific screen or level. Loading bundles in the background ensures assets are ready when needed without blocking the main thread. const manifest = { bundles: [ { name: 'home-screen', assets: [{ alias: 'flowerTop', src: 'https://pixijs.com/assets/flowerTop.png' }], }, { name: 'game-screen', assets: [{ alias: 'eggHead', src: 'https://pixijs.com/assets/eggHead.png' }], }, ], }; // Initialize with a manifest await Assets.init({ manifest }); // Start loading the game screen bundle in the background Assets.backgroundLoadBundle(['game-screen']); // Load only the first screen assets immediately const resources = await Assets.loadBundle('home-screen');

You can also load individual assets in the background using Assets.backgroundLoad(): // Register assets first Assets.add({ alias: 'flowerTop', src: 'https://pixijs.com/assets/flowerTop.png' }); Assets.add({ alias: 'eggHead', src: 'https://pixijs.com/assets/eggHead.png' }); // Load individual assets in the background Assets.backgroundLoad(['flowerTop', 'eggHead']);

Background-loaded assets may or may not be ready when you need them. Use Assets.load() to wait for completion; it returns immediately if the asset is already cached: // Start background loading early Assets.backgroundLoadBundle(['game-screen']); // Later, when the player navigates to the game screen: const resources = await Assets.loadBundle('game-screen'); // instant if already loaded
documents.s: Checking if an asset is ready

documents.t: Assets BackgroundLoader

Compressed textures use 4-8x less GPU memory than standard PNG/JPG textures and upload faster, especially on mobile devices or lower-end hardware. PixiJS supports multiple compressed texture formats, but you must register the appropriate loaders before using them.

Format File Extension Best for Description DDS .dds Desktop, S3TC hardware DirectDraw Surface format, supports DXT variants (S3TC) KTX .ktx Mobile (ETC2/ASTC) Khronos format, supports ETC and other schemes KTX2 .ktx2 Cross-platform (recommended) Supports Basis Universal and supercompressed formats Basis .basis Cross-platform, smallest files Highly compressed format that transcodes to multiple GPU formats

PixiJS does not include compressed texture support by default. Import the loaders you need before loading any assets: import 'pixi.js/dds'; import 'pixi.js/ktx'; import 'pixi.js/ktx2'; import 'pixi.js/basis'; note You only need to import loaders for the formats you use. These imports must run before any call to Assets.load.

Once loaders are registered, load compressed textures like any other asset: import 'pixi.js/ktx2'; import { Assets } from 'pixi.js'; await Assets.load('textures/background.ktx2'); PixiJS parses and uploads the texture using the correct loader and GPU-compatible transcoding path based on the user's device.

AssetPack supports automatic generation of compressed texture variants during your build step. You can: Convert .png or .jpg files into .basis, .ktx2, or .dds formats Reference compressed files in your manifest using the same aliases or wildcard patterns Use the same manifest and loading workflow; PixiJS resolves and loads the best variant based on the device

Your manifest can include multiple format candidates: { "bundles": [ { "name": "scene", "assets": [ { "alias": "bg", "src": ["assets/bg.ktx2", "assets/bg.basis", "assets/bg.png"] } ] } ] } PixiJS tries to load bg.ktx2 or bg.basis first if the device supports it, falling back to bg.png as needed.

Instead of loading assets one at a time, you can group them into bundles (e.g., "load screen", "level 1") and list those bundles in a manifest. This lets you load an entire screen's assets in one call and preload the next screen in the background.

A manifest is a descriptor object that defines your asset loading strategy. It lists bundles, each containing grouped assets by name and alias. This structure allows lazy-loading assets based on application context (e.g. load screen assets, level-specific content). const manifest = { bundles: [ { name: 'load-screen', assets: [ { alias: 'background', src: 'sunset.png' }, { alias: 'bar', src: 'load-bar.{png,webp}' }, // picks best format per device ], }, { name: 'game-screen', assets: [ { alias: 'character', src: 'robot.png' }, { alias: 'enemy', src: 'bad-guy.png' }, ], }, ], };

import { Assets } from 'pixi.js'; await Assets.init({ manifest }); Once initialized, load bundles by name: const loadScreenAssets = await Assets.loadBundle('load-screen'); const gameScreenAssets = await Assets.loadBundle('game-screen'); You can still load individual assets by alias without loading an entire bundle: await Assets.init({ manifest }); const background = await Assets.load('background'); const bar = await Assets.load('bar');
A bundle is a group of assets identified by a shared name. Bundles can be pre-defined in a manifest or registered dynamically at runtime.

import { Assets } from 'pixi.js'; Assets.addBundle('animals', [ { alias: 'bunny', src: 'bunny.png' }, { alias: 'chicken', src: 'chicken.png' }, { alias: 'thumper', src: 'thumper.png' }, ]); const assets = await Assets.loadBundle('animals'); // Or load a specific asset from the bundle const bunny = await Assets.load('bunny');
Managing manifests and bundles by hand is tedious and mistake-prone. AssetPack is a CLI tool that scans your assets folder and generates optimized manifests automatically.
